sens: Pleasing to the eye, having physical beauty
Well-suited to someone or something, appropriate or worthy
H5000.detail:
1. The word primarily describes what is beautiful, pleasant to look at: the woman in the Song of Songs is called "beautiful" (Song of Songs 1:5), even though she is tanned by the sun. It is a beauty that attracts, that charms.
2. However, it often also means what is "suitable" or "fitting" — what is appropriate to the situation or the person. Praise "suits" the righteous (Psalms 33:1), because it is fitting for them, it is worthy of them. Conversely, lies do not "suit" a noble (Proverbs 17:7), nor does glory suit a fool (Proverbs 26:1). It conveys the idea that something is in its place, that there is harmony between the person and what they do or possess.
H5000.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of what pleases, what is pleasant. It belongs to the family of Hebrew words describing beauty and suitability. Its primary meaning is visual and aesthetic, but it naturally extends to moral and social ideas: what is beautiful is also what is just, what is fitting.
H5000.emploi: This word appears 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Proverbs and the Song of Songs. In the Song, it describes the physical beauty of the beloved (1:5; 2:14; 4:3; 6:4). But more broadly, in Psalms and Proverbs, it expresses moral suitability: it is "fitting" to praise God when one is righteous (Psalms 33:1; 147:1), and it is not "suitable" for certain states or actions to be found in certain people (a fool with wealth or noble words). The word thus intertwines aesthetics and social order.
H5000.portee: This word reminds us that in the biblical vision, beauty and suitability go hand in hand. Praising God "suits" the believer: it is natural, it is just, it is beautiful. Conversely, certain actions are ugly, out of place, because they contradict who one is. This invites the reader to seek harmony between their faith and their life, between who they say they are and what they do.

sens: To pronounce a word as a prophet
To present one's own word as coming from God
To utter a false prophecy by usurping divine authority
H5001.detail:
1. The verb designates the fundamental act of the prophet: to pronounce a word, often solemnly. In Jeremiah 23:31, false prophets "give" their own word — they formulate it, publicly proclaim it — claiming that it comes from God.
2. There is a sense of transmission or attribution here: the prophet "gives" (presents, transmits) a word to his audience. When the word is authentic, it truly comes from the Lord; when it is false, the prophet gives his own thought by improperly appropriating it.
3. The prophetic context makes this verb serious: to "give" a false word in the name of God is a spiritual lie. Jeremiah 23:31 illustrates this distortion exactly: false prophets steal the title of ambassadors of God to validate their own imaginations.
H5001.origine: The Hebrew root suggests the idea of carrying, supporting, then expressing or proclaiming. In a prophetic context, the verb is enriched: the true prophet "carries" the word of God and "gives" it (transmits it faithfully); the false prophet also "gives," but by deceiving himself or deliberately misleading others.
H5001.emploi: This verb primarily appears in prophetic literature, notably in Jeremiah. The unique usage provided (Jeremiah 23:31) places it in a scathing critique of false prophets. The Lord denounces those who take "their own word" and "give" it as His — it is the usurpation of prophetic authority. The verb emphasizes the spiritual danger: confusing one's own thoughts with the word of God.
H5001.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us of the stakes of authenticity in proclaiming the Gospel. Anyone who speaks in God's name — pastor, preacher, prophet — must first listen faithfully before "giving" their word, that is, transmitting it. The risk of Jeremiah 23:31 remains current: passing off one's own desires or convictions as divine will. It is a call to humility and spiritual vigilance.

sens: Solemn declaration pronounced by a prophet in a state of divine inspiration
Phrase introducing or concluding a word that God makes known
Message or revelation that God entrusts to His prophet to convey to the people
H5002.detail:
1. It is primarily the word that the prophet pronounces when God seizes him and speaks through him. The prophet invents nothing: he transmits what the Lord has revealed to him, often in a particular state of inspiration or vision. Balaam sees this clearly in Numbers 24:3 and 24:4: he opens his eyes and speaks a word from the Lord that has manifested to him supernaturally.
2. The word also serves as a formula of seal or authenticity: when the text says "word of the Lord," it is like an official stamp certifying that this message truly comes from God, not from the prophet's imagination. In Genesis 22:16, the Lord Himself uses this word to solemnize His oath: He swears "by the word of the Lord," which shows the absolute authority behind these words.
3. This word is also what the prophet cries out or writes to warn, comfort, or judge the people in the name of God. Jeremiah, dozens of times, reports: "says the Lord" — it is the prophetic word that commands, threatens, or promises according to the situation of the people.
H5002.origine: The word comes from the root meaning "to pronounce, to emit a word." It is related to the idea of what comes out of the mouth — a living, active word, not just a sound. In the Old Testament, it is the specific term to distinguish the prophetic word from simple conversation: it carries the authority and power of God who pronounces it.
H5002.emploi: The word appears 358 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the prophets (Jeremiah alone contains it more than 150 times). It always appears in formula: "says the Lord" or "word of the Lord." Sometimes the prophet announces his vision or his word (Balaam in Numbers 24), but more often it is Jeremiah, Isaiah, or Ezekiel who use it to seal a divine word, often at the heart of an oracle of judgment or grace. The word is absent from simple narrative stories: it is reserved for moments when God speaks directly, when His intervention changes the course of events.
H5002.portee: This word reminds the reader that prophets do not speak in their own name, but as spokespersons of God. When encountering "word of the Lord," one knows they are receiving a direct communication from heaven, weighty, unavoidable — it is not a human opinion, it is a divine decree. For the Christian, this also shows how God has spoken to His people in a living and direct way throughout history: His word is never silent.

sens: To have sexual relations with another man's wife
To be unfaithful to one's spouse
To violate the marriage covenant
To worship other gods instead of the true God (figuratively)
H5003.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the illicit sexual act: a man who sleeps with another man's wife commits this act forbidden by God. It is a serious sin that violates another's marriage and the trust between spouses (Exodus 20:14: "You shall not commit adultery").
2. More broadly, it refers to being unfaithful in marriage, that is, betraying the commitment made to one's husband or wife. Leviticus 20:10 prescribes the death penalty for both guilty parties.
3. It is to violate the sacred covenant of marriage, breaking the bond of trust and fidelity that unites two spouses. Ezekiel 16:32 speaks of one who "has been an adulterous wife": she receives strangers instead of remaining faithful to her husband.
4. Figuratively, the Bible uses this word to describe Israel's unfaithfulness to God: the people "commit adultery" by worshiping other gods, turning to idolatry. Hosea 3:1 and Jeremiah 3:8 use this imagery to say that Israel betrays its covenant with the Lord just as an unfaithful wife betrays her husband.
H5003.origine: The Hebrew verb נָאַף (naph) has its root in the idea of breaking and violating a covenant. It describes the act by which one breaks the promised fidelity. The word has no direct etymological link to other verbs in the same family, but its use in the Bible makes it a specialized term for this violation of the marriage pact. The Hebrew language uses the imagery of marriage to speak of the covenant between God and His people, which explains why this verb also applies to idolatry.
H5003.emploi: This verb appears 26 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Jeremiah and Ezekiel. It is used to condemn marital unfaithfulness in the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in the wisdom literature of Israel (Proverbs, Job). The prophets use it extensively in a figurative sense: Jeremiah denounces Israel and Judah as adulterers (Jeremiah 9:2), Ezekiel takes up the image of the unfaithful wife for Jerusalem (Ezekiel 16:32), and Hosea uses the unfaithful marriage of Gomer as a parable for Israel's unfaithfulness to God. In all cases, the verb evokes a serious betrayal, a breaking of covenant, whether marital or spiritual.
H5003.portee: This word reminds us that the marriage covenant is sacred in God's eyes and that unfaithfulness is a serious sin. But its figurative use to describe idolatry invites the Christian to reflect on their own faithfulness to God: to worship other gods, serve mammon, or be seduced by the values of the world is to spiritually commit adultery. The word thus calls for loyalty, both in marriage and in the heart of faith.

sens: Sexual relationship outside of marriage, violation of marital commitment
Figuratively, unfaithfulness to God, idolatry
H5004.detail:
1. The word refers to the concrete act of sexual relations committed outside of marriage, particularly when a married person betrays their commitment. In Jeremiah 13:27, the prophet lists the sins of Jerusalem by referring to "adulteries" to denote the acts of sexual unfaithfulness for which the city was guilty.
2. The Bible also uses this word figuratively to describe idolatry: God's people are presented as a wife who abandons her commitment to her husband (God) to turn to other "lovers" (the idols). In Ezekiel 23:43, adultery represents Israel's persistent religious unfaithfulness as it continues to prostitute itself to idols despite its old age.
H5004.origine: The Hebrew word נִאֻף comes from a root that expresses the idea of transgression and violation of a covenant. It belongs to the family of words describing breaches of contract and commitment. The underlying image is that of tearing apart a bond that is supposed to be inviolable. This word applies both in the literal sense (carnal unfaithfulness) and in the figurative sense (unfaithfulness to God), showing how the Bible uses the language of marriage to express the covenant relationship between God and His people.
H5004.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament, both in the words of the prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel in the 6th century BC. In these two passages, it condemns not only the moral sins of sexual unfaithfulness but also, and especially, the systematic idolatry of the kingdom of Judah. Jeremiah uses it to enumerate the transgressions of Jerusalem, while Ezekiel employs it to describe the persistence of religious rebellion. The prophetic context shows that the word carries a moral and spiritual charge: it is not just about describing behavior, but about condemning it and calling for repentance.
H5004.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of the importance of fidelity in covenants, particularly the marital covenant. It also emphasizes that unfaithfulness to God — idolatry or abandonment of trust in Him — is presented in the Bible as being as serious and hurtful as marital betrayal. This comparison invites each believer to reflect on their own faithfulness to God and how they honor their commitments.

sens: act of sexual relations outside of marriage
marital unfaithfulness
betrayal of the covenant bond between spouses
H5005.detail:
1. The word refers to the physical act of sexual relations committed outside of marriage: it is a serious offense that violates the marital contract. In Hosea 2:4, the prophet reproaches Israel (the image of the unfaithful people) for its "adulteries," meaning its betrayals of the covenant with God, compared to the unfaithfulness of a wife.
2. Figuratively, in biblical thought, adultery is not just a sexual sin: it represents spiritual unfaithfulness, a failure to uphold the covenant. Israel, wed to God, commits "adultery" by turning to idols and abandoning its commitment to the Lord.
H5005.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of defilement and violation. It is related to the concept of unfaithfulness that breaks a sacred bond. This image of the unfaithful people compared to an adulterous wife is particularly developed by the prophets, especially Hosea, to express the rupture of the covenant between God and Israel.
H5005.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Hosea 2:4. The prophet Hosea uses it in a context of divine controversy: God calls the people to judge their mother (Israel, the community) who has engaged in idolatry and unfaithfulness. The plural "adulteries" reinforces the idea of multiple betrayals. This usage shows how the vocabulary of marital unfaithfulness becomes a theological language for the prophets to describe the apostasy of the people.
H5005.portee: This word reminds the believer that the covenant with God is like a marriage: it requires fidelity and exclusivity. Turning away from God to seek elsewhere (riches, idols, powers) is a form of serious unfaithfulness. It is an invitation to examine our own loyalties and to remain committed to the engagement we have made with the Lord.

sens: Reject something or someone with disdain, consider them unworthy
Deliberately refuse to respect a person, a law, or a covenant
Show insolence towards God, insult His honor
Treat something as worthless, disdain it
H5006.detail:
1. To despise someone or something is to reject it with a deep sense of disdain, as if it were worthless. It is the attitude of the heart that lowers someone or something beneath oneself. In Numbers 14:11, Moses reproaches the people for despising the Lord by not believing in His wonders.

2. It is also to refuse to respect what should be honored: a person, a law, a covenant. The one who despises acts with insolence, deliberately opposing an established order. In Deuteronomy 31:20, the people will despise the covenant that God has made with them and turn to other gods.

3. Despising takes on a particularly serious dimension when the object is God or His honor. The word can then be translated as "blaspheme": it is to insult the divine name, treating it as unworthy of reverence. In 2 Samuel 12:14, David, through his sin with Bathsheba, caused the Lord to be blasphemed by his enemies.

4. To disdain is also to refuse to consider, to reject with a sort of grimace. In Proverbs 1:30, the foolish have despised the counsel of wisdom, refusing to listen to or take it seriously.
H5006.origine: The Hebrew verb נָאַץ comes from a root that expresses the idea of rejecting, pushing away. The basic image is that of a violent movement that drives something far from oneself. The word is used in several verbal forms, which intensify or nuance this idea of rejection: simple disdain, disdain caused to others, or the act of being despised. The family of this word in Hebrew shares this same notion of rejection with force and energy.
H5006.emploi: This verb appears 24 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books, the Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophets. The uses show that the subject of disdain is often God Himself or His attributes: His name, His covenant, His law. Sometimes, it is an adversary who despises God (Psalms 74:10: the enemy will despise the name of God). Sometimes, it is the people who despise the Lord by refusing to believe or by following other gods (Isaiah 1:4). Disdain can also target wisdom (Proverbs 1:30) or the established order (Numbers 16:30). Each time, it is a serious act of rebellion or insolence, a break of respect towards what is holy or established.
H5006.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp the seriousness of sin in the Bible. Despising is not simple indifference: it is an active and proud refusal to recognize God's authority or His holiness. It shows that turning away from God is never neutral; it is always an insult to His honor. This word challenges the Christian regarding their attitudes towards God and His word: are we truly submissive, or do we find excuses to disdain His commandments?

sens: Insult or derogatory word addressed to someone
Shame, dishonor that results from it
Public disdain, mockery directed against a person or a people
H5007A.detail: 1. Reproach is primarily an insult, a word of disdain thrown at someone to offend and humiliate them. It is the act of one who belittles, who mocks. 2. This word also denotes the shame and dishonor that follow: when one suffers reproach, they bear its mark, losing their dignity in the eyes of others. 3. Finally, it is the public disdain and collective ridicule of a people or a nation that has been defeated: in Isaiah 37:3, Hezekiah describes a day of reproach, when besieged Jerusalem suffers the insult of the Assyrian army and risks losing its honor before all nations.
H5007A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to despise" or "to reject." It expresses the idea of pushing someone away with disdain, treating them as unworthy. The form נְאָצָה is a spelling variant of נֶאָצָה (H5007B); both express exactly the same meaning and appear in the biblical text.
H5007A.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages that describe the same scene: the moment when Hezekiah receives the envoys of the king of Assyria who come to demand the surrender of Jerusalem. In these two verses (2 Kings 19:3 and Isaiah 37:3), reproach denotes the insult and shame that the enemy inflicts on Judah, in a situation of extreme distress where the kingdom seems on the brink of collapse. The context is one of military threat and national humiliation.
H5007A.portee: Reproach reminds the reader that the people of God can experience shame and humiliation before their enemies, and that this trial is a form of judgment. But it is also a call to trust: in these verses, Hezekiah turns to God at the very moment when reproach threatens, showing that deliverance comes from God alone, not from human forces.

sens: Derogatory word or act towards someone
Insult, injury directed against a person or against God
Blasphemous mockery, insolent rejection of an authority or a covenant
H5007B.detail:
1. Outrage is a word or action that belittles someone, humiliating them publicly with disdain. In Nehemiah 9:18, the people of Israel commit outrages against God by making a golden calf: it is a direct insult to the one who has just freed them from Egypt, an affront to His glory.
2. It is also the insult directed against a person, often to make them ridiculous or to hurt them. In Ezekiel 35:12, God lists the outrages that Edom has hurled against the mountains of Israel, that is, against the people of Israel themselves, words of disdain and triumph.
3. At a more serious level, outrage becomes a mocking rejection of a covenant or legitimate authority. In Nehemiah 9:26, the Israelites commit great outrages by rebelling against God, throwing His law behind their backs and killing His prophets — it is an active blasphemy, an insult to the very face of the Lord.
H5007B.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of rejecting, despising, treating without respect. The family of this word always carries this nuance of affront or denial. Outrage is less a simple insult than a deliberate attack on someone's honor or dignity, particularly when it targets God or His authority.
H5007B.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe acts or words of rebellion against the Lord. In Nehemiah 9, in a prayer of repentance, the people acknowledge the great outrages they have committed by worshiping a molten calf and rebelling against God. In Ezekiel 35, God denounces the outrages of the nation of Edom, which has dared to insult the mountains of Israel and rejoice in its downfall. In all cases, outrage is a voluntary act, laden with arrogance and disdain, a transgression that directly affects God's honor.
H5007B.portee: This word reminds the reader that rejecting God or His prophets is not a simple disagreement: it is a personal affront directed at the one who created us and loves us. Outrages against God make us aware that rebellion is never neutral — it insults, it hurts, it rejects the relationship that God offers. Acknowledging our outrages, as the Israelites do in Nehemiah 9, is a step towards sincere repentance.

sens: To emit a groan, a plaintive sound from deep in the throat
To express one's suffering or agony through inarticulate cries
H5008.detail:
1. The verb describes the involuntary groaning, that deep and muffled cry that one emits despite oneself when experiencing physical pain. In Job 24:12, the dying in the cities "exhale sighs," as if their life and pain escape in the form of complaints. It is the natural sound of one who is agonizing or enduring intolerable suffering.
2. The word is used to express extreme agony or humiliation before a superior force. In Ezekiel 30:24, Pharaoh "will groan" before the king of Babylon "like the dying groan" — an image of total helplessness and crushing defeat, when the vanquished can only whimper under the weight of their ruin.
H5008.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes a guttural, deep, and inarticulate sound. It is related to other Hebrew words that describe cries of pain or lamentation. The basic image is that of an involuntary cry torn from the throat by suffering, a sound that one cannot control.
H5008.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 24:12, it describes the sighs of the dying who are exploited, forgotten by God — a call to conscience in the face of injustice. In Ezekiel 30:24, it paints the agony of the defeated and humiliated Pharaoh. The use remains linked to extreme physical or moral suffering, at the moment when words fade before the cry of the wounded flesh.
H5008.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the suffering of humanity — it presents it to us in its raw reality. The groans of the victims are never completely invisible to God, even if the psalmist or the prophet sometimes contests this. It is a word for those who suffer in silence: their cry, even if unarticulated, exists and matters.

sens: A deep and painful cry emitted under suffering
A complaint expressing distress and oppression
An expression of compassion in the face of the misery of others
H5009.detail:
1. Groaning is that deep, restrained cry that someone emits when suffering intensely — not a piercing scream, but a prolonged and muffled complaint. It is the sound of one who is in agony or injured. In Ezekiel 30:24, Pharaoh "will groan before him as the dying groan": the image is that of a man in agony, producing those muffled sounds at the end of his breath.
2. Groaning also expresses oppression, servitude, and collective misery. In Exodus 2:24 and 6:5, the children of Israel groan under the Egyptian yoke: these are not articulated words, but complaints torn from suffering and humiliation. The groaning rises from a crushed heart.
3. Groaning can also reflect the compassion of one who hears someone suffering. In Judges 2:18, the Lord "had pity on their groanings" — the word here designates the complaint of the oppressed, but also invites us to grasp the mercy of the one who listens and acts.
H5009.origine: The Hebrew word נְאָקָה comes from a root that evokes the muffled and inarticulate sound of suffering — a groan, a moan. It is a word that primarily paints the sound, the voice of the body in distress, rather than the words of the heart. The term belongs to the vocabulary of affliction and silent cries.
H5009.emploi: The word appears four times in the Old Testament, always to evoke the distress of Israel or an oppressed person. In Exodus 2:24 and 6:5, the groans of the Hebrew slaves rise to God and prompt Him to remember His covenant and free His people. In Judges 2:18, it is the Lord's compassion in response to the groaning of His oppressed people that leads Him to send them saviors. In Ezekiel 30:24, it is the sound of agony. Each time, the groaning is a sign of real suffering that calls out.
H5009.portee: Groaning reminds us that God hears even what is not expressed in words — the muffled complaints, the silent pain, the voiceless misery. When one cries without being able to speak, when one weeps without being heard by the world, the Lord listens to our groanings and is moved. It is a word that tells us that our silent sufferings do not remain invisible to God.

sens: to reject with contempt
to push away what one had accepted
to show disgust or aversion for something
H5010.detail: 1. To despise means to reject something or someone with contempt, as one pushes away what disgusts them. It is to actively scorn, to turn away from what one deems unworthy. 2. This verb also designates the act of rejecting or abandoning what one had previously accepted or chosen: thus God despises the covenant He had made, or He despises the altar where He was served (Lamentations 2:7). It is a rejection that is all the more serious as it breaks an established bond. 3. The word expresses disgust, aversion: it is to manifest through actions (and not just words) that one finds something repugnant or unworthy of being kept.
H5010.origine: The Hebrew verb נאר (ná'ar) comes from a root that expresses the idea of rejecting or shaking off. The form used in the Bible (Piel) intensifies the meaning: it is not a simple turning away of the gaze, but an active and vigorous rejection. The word belongs to the family of expressions that describe disgust and aversion in daily life and in relation to God.
H5010.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It is used to express the action by which God despises or pushes away what should be dear to Him: His covenant with David (Psalms 89:40) and His own altar (Lamentations 2:7). In both cases, it is a moment of rupture and judgment: God rejects what was sacred, as a sign of His wrath and the temporary abandonment of His people. The context is always that of a deep spiritual crisis.
H5010.portee: This word reminds us that God's rejection is never light or arbitrary: when He despises, it is in reaction to the sin and infidelity of His people. For the believer, these passages teach us to take seriously the covenant with God and not to assume that His favor is guaranteed without obedience. They also invite us to recognize that even in judgment, God remains just.

sens: priestly city of Judah, north of Jerusalem
high place or dominant position
H5011.detail: 1. Nob is a city inhabited by priests, notably Ahimelech. David takes refuge there to obtain consecrated bread when he flees from Saul (1 Samuel 21:1). It is there that Doeg denounces David to the king (1 Samuel 22:9), which leads to the massacre ordered by Saul: all the priests of Nob, men, women, and children, are killed by the sword (1 Samuel 22:19). 2. The name means "high place," evoking a city on an elevation. Isaiah mentions Nob as a stopping point where the Assyrian army threatens Jerusalem from a height (Isaiah 10:32), highlighting its dominant position near the capital.
H5011.origine: The Hebrew name נֹב (nov) literally means "high place" or "elevation," from a root that evokes the idea of height or elevated position. This etymology fits its geographical situation: Nob was located on a height north of Jerusalem, giving it a strategic and visible position.
H5011.emploi: Nob appears 6 times in the Bible, primarily in the account of 1 Samuel 21—22. It is a city of priests, a religious center where David seeks refuge and food from the priest Ahimelech. The major event is the massacre of all its inhabitants by order of Saul, who is enraged by the help given to David (1 Samuel 22:19): this drama profoundly marks Saul's history and illustrates the cruelty that overtakes him. Nob is also mentioned in the territorial lists of Nehemiah 11:32 among the cities reoccupied after the exile, and in Isaiah 10:32 as a landmark on the path that the Assyrian army would follow.
H5011.portee: Nob symbolizes the fragility of holy places in the face of persecution: its innocent priests pay the price for their hospitality towards David. This massacre reveals how Saul, driven by jealousy and fear, descends into tyranny and becomes a murderer of those who serve the Lord. For the believer, Nob reminds us that faithful service to God can attract the world's opposition, but that God's story continues despite these destructions.

sens: Speak in the name of God, convey His inspired message
Express oneself under the impulse of the divine Spirit
Announce the future or the will of God
Predict false things while claiming to be a prophet
Exercise the role, the function of a prophet
H5012.detail:
1. To prophesy is to speak in the name of God to convey His message to the people. This is what true prophets, filled with the Spirit of the Lord, do: to the seventy elders of Israel, the Spirit of God "came upon them, and they prophesied" (Numbers 11:25), meaning they pronounced the divine word.
2. The prophet speaks under the direct impulse of the Spirit, not of his own will. It is an intense experience: Ezekiel reports, "I prophesied as I was commanded. And as I prophesied, there was a noise" (Ezekiel 37:7), showing that prophecy accompanies divine action.
3. To prophesy can also mean to announce the future or the will of God, particularly judgment or salvation. The king asks the prophet, "Do not prophesy anything good concerning me; he only prophesies evil" (1 Kings 22:18), which shows that a prophet is expected to speak about what is to come.
4. The term also applies to false prophets who claim to speak in the name of God without having received the command. Jeremiah denounces those "who prophesy lies" (Jeremiah 20:6) and those "who prophesy peace concerning Jerusalem, when there is no peace" (Ezekiel 13:16).
5. To prophesy is to fulfill the charge, the ministry of the prophet within the community of Israel, proclaiming the word of the Lord to kings, priests, and the people.
H5012.origine: The Hebrew verb נָבָא (nava) comes from a root that expresses the idea of gushing forth, flowing, or rising — like a spring that bursts forth. The image is that of a word rising from the heart and gushing from the mouth, driven by the Spirit of God. The root also appears in the word "prophet" (נָבִיא, navi). Most biblical usages concern the action of receiving and transmitting the divine word, rather than mere prediction; it is an active and living act.
H5012.emploi: The verb to prophesy appears more than 100 times in biblical Hebrew, particularly in the books of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, where it describes the central activity of the prophet. At the beginning of Israel's history, in 1 Samuel 10, the verb characterizes the experience of young Saul filled with the Spirit, who "prophesied" (1 Samuel 10:10). Later, it becomes the key word to express the ministry of the great prophets: Jeremiah and Ezekiel claim it as their vocation. The context varies according to the prophet: true prophets prophesy what the Lord commands them, while false prophets prophesy without having received a mandate (Jeremiah 14:14; 23:16), highlighting the critical importance of the source and authority of the prophetic word.
H5012.portee: This word teaches Christians that biblical prophecy is primarily a ministry of proclamation — announcing the word of God to men — rather than a mere prediction. It presupposes the living action of the Spirit, not an effort of man alone. The word also reminds us that true prophecy is distinguished from false by its source: it comes from God, not from the prophet's imagination. For the Christian reader, this sheds light on the role of the prophet as God's spokesperson in the Old Testament and raises the question of authenticity: where does the word truly come from?

sens: Pronounce words that come from God
Transmit a divine message as a prophet
H5013.detail: 1. To prophesy is to pronounce words that come directly from God. The prophet does not speak from himself, but is carried by the Spirit of God to announce His will, warnings, or promises. 2. It is also to exercise the function of a prophet: to convey God's message to a people or a king. In the account of Ezra, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah prophesy to the Jews returned from exile (Ezra 5:1), encouraging them to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.
H5013.origine: The Aramaic verb נְבָא (ne.va) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word נָבָא (na.va, verb no. 5012), both meaning "to prophesy." This root evokes the notion of speaking in someone else's name, conveying a message that does not come from oneself. In Aramaic and Hebrew, the root nby- is related to the idea of announcement and divine proclamation.
H5013.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible in Aramaic: in Ezra 5:1, where it says that "the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, son of Iddo, prophesied." This is a key moment: after the return from exile in Babylon, these two prophets encourage the people to resume the construction of the temple that the Persians had interrupted. The context shows that to prophesy here means to bring a word from God to restart and support the divine project.
H5013.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that the prophet is not a fortune teller or magician, but a messenger of God. To prophesy is to convey what God says, not to invent or guess. This underscores the importance of listening to God's voice and communicating it faithfully to others.

sens: Have a cavity inside, be empty
Made with thin walls around an empty space
Contrary or opposite (figurative sense)
H5014.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of something emptied from the inside, which has an empty space within its volume: the altar of the Tabernacle in Exodus 27:8 is built "hollow, with boards," meaning it is not a solid block, but a hollow structure that can be transported more easily.
2. More concretely, "hollow" describes something shaped so that it is light and portable: the bars that go through the rings of this hollow altar in Exodus 38:7 allow it to be lifted and moved, which would not have been possible if it had been solid.
3. In a figurative or ironic context, the word can mean what is contrary or vain: in Job 11:12, the man "contrary to" the animal possesses intelligence, but the fool remains without wisdom — here the word expresses a kind of contradiction or absence of what should be present.
H5014.origine: The Hebrew root נָבַב (navav) is related to the idea of digging or hollowing out. It belongs to the family of words that describe states of absence or emptiness — from the same root comes the name "nob," which can designate a hollow substance or an emptiness. The starting image is that of the hollow of a hand, a cavity: something that has lost its fullness or solidity to become porous or empty.
H5014.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively to describe the furniture of the Tabernacle. In Exodus 27:8 and 38:7, it applies to the altar of burnt offerings, which must be built hollow to be transported during the people's movements in the desert — this is a practical and theological requirement of itinerant worship. Only once, in Jeremiah 52:21, it applies to temple columns. In Job 11:12, the word takes on a metaphorical or contrastive sense, speaking of what is "contrary" — this passage shows an extension of the concrete meaning towards the idea of absence or opposition. The Old Testament usage remains focused on physical description.
H5014.portee: For the believer, this requirement that the altar be hollow reminds us of a spiritual lesson: the place of encounter with God must be mobile, devoid of unnecessary weight, ready to follow divine guidance. A solid and massive altar would suggest a definitive earthly stability; a hollow altar indicates that true worship is not attached to any fixed place, but follows the Word of God. This is a concrete detail that teaches the freedom and obedience of the heart.

sens: City of Moab located in Transjordan
Fortified locality inhabited and built by the tribes of Israel
Mountainous region associated with the lamentations of Moab
H5015A.detail: 1. Nebo is a city of Moab, a region located east of the Jordan. It is mentioned as one of the cities that the children of Reuben and Gad wished to conquer and inhabit during the conquest of Canaan (Numbers 32:3). 2. The Israelites rebuilt and fortified this city: Numbers 32:38 reports that the tribes changed the names of the cities they rebuilt, including Nebo. 3. The city is also associated with the mountain of Abarim, where Israel camped during its journey in the desert (Numbers 33:47), and it represents a territorial boundary of the Reubenite kingdom (1 Chronicles 5:8). 4. In the prophecies against Moab, Nebo is cited as a place of lamentation and destruction, ravaged by divine judgment (Isaiah 15:2 and Jeremiah 48:1).
H5015A.origine: The name Nebo means "prophet" in Hebrew. It is a term that evokes the transmission of divine word. The city bears this prestigious name, although the exact origin of the link between the name and the locality remains uncertain. It is probably located on or near Mount Nebo, a high-altitude region in Transjordan.
H5015A.emploi: Nebo appears seven times in the Bible, exclusively in the Old Testament. It is first mentioned in the context of the conquest and division of the lands (Numbers 32-33), where Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh request to settle in Transjordan. Then, it appears as a territorial boundary of the Reubenite kingdom (1 Chronicles 5:8). Finally, it features in the oracles of judgment against Moab pronounced by Isaiah and Jeremiah (Isaiah 15:2 and Jeremiah 48:1, 22), where it symbolizes the Moabite cities struck by misfortune.

sens: Babylonian deity of knowledge and writing
H5015B.detail: Nebo is the name of a Babylonian god worshiped by the Babylonians as the god of learning, wisdom, and writing. His name means "prophet" in Babylonian. The Babylonians revered him as the one who presides over letters and knowledge. The prophet Isaiah mentions him in Isaiah 46:1 to show the collapse of the Babylonian gods in the face of the true God: "Bel bows down, Nebo stoops," highlighting that even the deities worshiped by Babylon have no power and fall under God's judgment.
H5015B.origine: Nebo comes from the Babylonian god Nabu, whose name means "prophet" or "one who speaks." This god was highly revered in ancient Babylon, associated with the god Marduk as his son. In the Babylonian pantheon, he embodied wisdom and mastery of writing. The name has been transliterated into Hebrew as Nebo to designate this foreign deity.
H5015B.emploi: Nebo appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 46:1. The prophet Isaiah mentions him in a context of judgment on Babylon: he announces that the gods of Babylon, including Nebo and Bel, collapse and fall. Their idols are placed on beasts of burden, becoming a weight for the weary animals. Isaiah uses this mention to mock the Babylonian gods and show their powerlessness before the true God of Israel. It is a moment of contrast: while the false gods fall, the God of Israel remains sovereign.
H5015B.portee: This mention of Nebo reminds the reader that false gods, no matter their reputation for wisdom and power, have no true substance and collapse. For a Christian, it emphasizes that true knowledge and true wisdom come from the living God, not from idols or false teachings of the world. This word encourages the believer not to fear the religious or ideological systems of the powers of this world.

sens: City of Judea from which families of exiles returned from Babylon
Name of a family or clan whose members returned with Zerubbabel
H5015G.detail:
1. Nebo is a city located in Judea (possibly at the border of Benjamin) mentioned during the return of the exiles from Babylon under the leadership of Zerubbabel. Ezra 2:29 and Nehemiah 7:33 list "the people of Nebo" or "the sons of Nebo" among those who returned to Jerusalem, numbering fifty-two.
2. Nebo also refers to the clan or family originating from this city: Ezra 10:43 mentions "the sons of Nebo" among those who had separated from their foreign wives, showing that this designation encompasses both the place and the family group that originated from it.
H5015G.origine: The name Nebo probably means "prophet" in Hebrew. Nebo is found in biblical geography: a mountain of the same name exists in Transjordan (Mount Nebo), but this city of Judea is distinct. The name of the family or clan bears the same name as its city of origin, a common practice in lists of return from exile.
H5015G.emploi: Nebo appears three times in the Bible, all in texts related to the return from exile in the fifth century B.C. It is found in the lists of Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, which enumerate the families returned from captivity with Zerubbabel. The constant number of fifty-two people (Ezra 2:29 and Nehemiah 7:33) indicates the numerical importance of this clan among the repatriates. Ezra 10:43 shows that members of this family had to address issues of mixed marriage, revealing their active role in the restored community.
H5015G.portee: Nebo reminds us that the return from exile was not a purely spiritual event: real families, with their names, histories, and concrete challenges, rebuilt the people of God. This detail shows that God cares for each individual, including those whose names might be forgotten, and that the restoration of the people took place step by step, family by family.

sens: Mountain located east of the Jordan, facing Jericho
Summit where Moses died after seeing the Promised Land
H5015H.detail: 1. Nebo is a steep mountain rising east of the Jordan, in the region of Moab, directly opposite Jericho, the city that the Israelites were to conquer. It is a well-known geographical landmark for the people of God. 2. It is on Nebo, at the summit called Pisgah, that Moses ascends at the end of his life to behold the entire Promised Land before dying. The Lord shows him the full extent from the Negev to Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:1). This place symbolizes the moment when Moses, after forty years of wandering in the desert, finally sees the fulfillment of the promise without entering it himself.
H5015H.origine: The name Nebo means "prophet" in Hebrew. It thus bears the name of the prophetic ministry, for it is here that God grants Moses, the greatest prophet of Israel, a final and extraordinary vision of the territory promised to his people before his death. This mountain is also called Abarim, which means "the passages" or "the mountains on the other side."
H5015H.emploi: Nebo appears twice in Deuteronomy, always in connection with the death of Moses. In Deuteronomy 32:49, God commands Moses to go up this mountain of Abarim to see the land. In Deuteronomy 34:1, the account tells that Moses indeed goes up Mount Nebo, at the summit of Pisgah, where the Lord shows him all the land. These two passages form a coherent and solemn account of the leader's last moment before his death.
H5015H.portee: Nebo reminds the reader that even the greatest servants of God do not always possess what they have served for all their lives. Moses sees the promise from afar without possessing it, which underscores the importance of faith in God rather than in our own accomplishments. It is a call to trust: God sees further than we do and fulfills his promises, even beyond our human limits.

sens: Message or teaching received from God and conveyed by a prophet
Written work or collection containing a divine revelation
False prediction or one made without God's mandate
H5016.detail:
1. Prophecy is primarily the message that God addresses to His people through the mouth of a prophet. It is an authentic divine word, delivered by someone whom God has sent. In 2 Chronicles 15:8, when Asa hears "the prophecy of Obed the prophet," it refers to a true divine message that compels him to transform an entire kingdom.

2. A prophecy can also refer to the written work or book in which these revelations are gathered. In 2 Chronicles 9:29, the "prophecy of Ahijah of Shiloh" refers to a collection of divine teachings transmitted by this prophet — a text that could be consulted.

3. By extension, the term can apply to a prophetic word that does not originate from God: it is then a false prophecy. In Nehemiah 6:12, when Shemaiah "prophesied" against Nehemiah for money, it was a lie presented in the guise of a divine message — a deceptive prophecy.
H5016.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root of "prophet" (nabi), which designates one who speaks on behalf of God or announces the future. Prophecy is therefore literally "the action and content of the prophetic word." It is a word of the same family as the verb "to prophesy," which means "to speak as a prophet." This concept is central in the Old Testament: the prophet is the authorized spokesperson of the Lord to the people.
H5016.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. Twice, it designates an authentic prophecy: in 2 Chronicles 9:29, among the historical sources of Solomon's reign; in 2 Chronicles 15:8, where it leads King Asa to repentance. A third time, in Nehemiah 6:12, the term applies to a false prophetic word, pronounced for monetary gain by a man of ill intent. The three uses show that the word can qualify both a true word from God and a fraudulent counterfeit.
H5016.portee: For the Christian reader, the word reminds us that authentic prophecy transforms a life and a people: it calls for justice and conversion. It also invites discernment: not every word that presents itself as prophetic is necessarily from God. It can be a self-serving lie, as in Nehemiah 6:12. That is why the Bible invites us to "test the spirits."

sens: Message or word that God communicates through a prophet
Written work or collection containing the prophetic words of a messenger from God
H5017.detail:
1. Prophecy is primarily a divine word transmitted by a prophet to his people. In Ezra 6:14, we speak of the "prophecies" of Haggai and Zechariah, the two prophets who encouraged the Jews to rebuild the Temple after the exile. These words from God provided strength and authority to the project.
2. The word also designates the prophetic writing itself, the book or collection where these words are recorded. The prophecies of Haggai and Zechariah have become sacred texts that the Jews followed to obey God's will.
H5017.origine: The Aramaic word נְבוּאָה comes from the same root as the Hebrew נְבוּאָה (H5016), which means "prophecy." This root is related to the verb נָבָא ("to prophesy"), whose primary meaning is "to speak in the name of God" or "to announce." The initial image is that of a word that goes out and spreads, coming from a divine source and passing through the mouth of the prophet.
H5017.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible in Aramaic, in Ezra 6:14. The historical context is crucial: after the exile in Babylon, the Jewish people return and undertake to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem. It is a time of doubt and difficulty. The prophecies of Haggai and Zechariah — two contemporary prophets — revive the project with words of encouragement and divine direction. The word "prophecy" emphasizes that these are not mere human advice, but words inspired by God Himself, which give legitimacy and strength to the project.
H5017.portee: For the Christian reader, prophecy reminds us that God never leaves His people without guidance. Even in dark times — exile, ruin, doubt — He raises up prophets to restore and lead them. It is a sign that the word of God is alive, present, and effective in history. This encourages us to listen to what God says through His Word rather than to follow fear or despair.

sens: Chief of the guards of the king of Babylon at the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.
Babylonian officer responsible for the capture and deportation of the Judeans
Man who executes the orders of Nebuchadnezzar in the conquered city
H5018.detail:
1. Nebuzaradan is the Babylonian general whom King Nebuchadnezzar sends to lead the final assault against Jerusalem: he enters the city on the seventh day of the fifth month of the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign (2 Kings 25:8), as the "chief of the guards" — a title that designates him as responsible for the king's elite military.

2. He fulfills the functions of military administrator of the conquered territory: he arrests important survivors and leads them to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah for judgment (2 Kings 25:20), but he also spares the poorest, to whom he entrusts vineyards and fields (Jeremiah 39:10). He thus appears as the executive arm of Babylonian power on the ground.

3. The texts show him in direct dialogue with the prophet Jeremiah, whom he treats with honor and freedom, highlighting his central role in post-destruction operations and his own authority in Judean affairs (Jeremiah 40:1).
H5018.origine: The Babylonian name Nebuzaradan means "Nebo has given a seed" (Nebo was a Babylonian god). It is an honorific title combining the name of the patron god and the affirmation of fertility or succession. Historically, this character is attested in Babylonian annals as a high-ranking general under Nebuchadnezzar II.
H5018.emploi: Nebuzaradan appears 15 times in the Bible, primarily in 2 Kings 25 and in the book of Jeremiah (chapters 39-52). In chapters 25 and 39 of Jeremiah, then 2 Kings 25, he figures as the military chief who executes the siege and destruction of Jerusalem. In Jeremiah 39-40, his role extends to governing the territory: he spares the poor and entrusts Jeremiah to Gedaliah (Jeremiah 40:1-5), showing a certain clemency. He represents the power and administrative efficiency of Babylon, but also, in Jeremiah's view, the possibility of humane treatment towards the conquered.
H5018.portee: Nebuzaradan embodies the execution of God's judgment on Jerusalem through a foreign power. His presence reminds the reader that the God of Israel controls the history of empires to accomplish His purposes. His respect for Jeremiah and his clemency towards the poor also show that God's grace manifests even in the midst of captivity, protecting the prophet and preserving a human remnant.

sens: Great king of Babylon who ruled in the 6th century B.C.
Monarch who conquered Jerusalem and deported the people of Judah into captivity
Instrument of God's judgment on unfaithful Israel and Judah
H5019.detail:
1. Nebuchadnezzar is the powerful king of the Babylonian empire who reigns at a time when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah are weakening. His name means "may Nebo protect the crown" (Nebo was a Babylonian deity). He becomes the great political and military figure of the Near East during this period.

2. He is best known for besieging Jerusalem, capturing King Jehoiakim, and deporting thousands of Judeans to Babylon. In 2 Kings 24:1, we learn that he "went up against" and that Jehoiakim "became his servant." He also takes the treasures of the temple and establishes a puppet king on the throne of Judah.

3. In the message of the prophets, particularly Jeremiah, Nebuchadnezzar appears as an instrument in God's hand to punish the unfaithfulness of Judah. Jeremiah 27:6 calls him the servant of the Lord: it is through him that God executes His judgment on His rebellious people. His military campaigns, although motivated by political ambition, fulfill divine purpose.
H5019.origine: The name comes from the Akkadian "Nabu-kudurri-uṣur," which literally means "may Nebo protect the firstborn" or "may Nebo protect the crown." Nebo was the Babylonian god of wisdom and writing. The historical king bore this name from birth as an act of devotion to this deity. The Hebrew Scriptures adopt it as is, thus acknowledging its historical reality while the biblical context redefines its function: not as a protected one of a false deity, but as an unconscious executor of the will of the true God.
H5019.emploi: Nebuchadnezzar is mentioned 59 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical books (2 Kings, 2 Chronicles) and in the prophet Jeremiah (over 30 occurrences). The early accounts (2 Kings 24-25, 2 Chronicles 36) recount the phases of his invasion: first Jehoiakim submits (2 Kings 24:1), then the siege of Jerusalem leads to the fall of the city and the first deportation (Jeremiah 24:1, 29:1). Jeremiah conveys divine messages threatening the kings of Judah who refuse to submit to Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 21:7, 27:6-8, 34:1-2). The last mentions (Jeremiah 52, Ezekiel 26-30) place his reign as a key moment when the kingdoms of the Levant fall under his domination. His role is consistent: a ruthless conqueror from a political standpoint, an agent of divine judgment from a theological perspective.
H5019.portee: Nebuchadnezzar teaches the reader that God controls world history, even through powers that ignore Him. Judah has sinned greatly by turning away from God; that is why God allowed this distant king to conquer and exile them. This judgment is not the final word: prophets announce a return of the exiled people (Jeremiah 29, Ezekiel). Thus, Nebuchadnezzar reminds us that faithfulness to God produces peace, while unfaithfulness brings His judgment, but also that God never rejects His people forever.

sens: King of Babylon who destroyed Jerusalem and exiled Judah
Powerful sovereign who conquered the people of God
Pagan monarch confronted with the miracles of the God of Israel
H5020.detail:
1. Nebuchadnezzar is the great king of Babylon who, in the 6th century B.C., conquered Jerusalem and deported the people of Judah into exile. Ezra 5:12 presents him as the one who "destroyed this house" (the temple) "and carried the people captive to Babylon." This is a decisive moment in the history of Israel: God's judgment on the unfaithfulness of the people.

2. In the book of Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar appears as a powerful king who erects a golden statue and demands that all bow down before it (Daniel 3:5-14). He represents human authority that opposes God and claims worship that belongs only to God alone.

3. However, Nebuchadnezzar is also a king whom God instructs through signs and miracles. He sees his three young servants miraculously saved from the fire (Daniel 3:26), and he comes to recognize the power of the God of Israel: "the Most High God" who protects His faithful servants.
H5020.origine: The name means "may Nebo protect the crown" (Nebo being a Babylonian deity). This is the name that the Babylonians gave to this historical monarch, also known by the Greek name Nebuchadnezzar. The biblical text designates him as the great king of Babylon, and his reign spans several decades in the 6th century B.C.
H5020.emploi: Nebuchadnezzar is mentioned 29 times in the Bible, primarily in the books of Ezra and Daniel. In Ezra 5:12 and 6:5, he is recalled as the one who destroyed the temple of Jerusalem and exiled Judah, but also as the king who took the sacred vessels from the temple. The book of Daniel shows him throughout its first four chapters: he orders the worship of the golden statue, throws the three young Hebrews into the fiery furnace, and gradually recognizes the greatness of the God of Israel through dreams and miracles (Daniel 2:46, 4:18, 4:37). His character embodies the confrontation between human political power and the sovereignty of God.
H5020.portee: Nebuchadnezzar reminds the reader that human empires, no matter how powerful, cannot stand against the God of Israel. His story also teaches that even a pagan king can gradually recognize the true power of God when he sees His works: it encourages us to remain faithful to God in all circumstances, even in the face of hostile powers.

sens: Babylonian officer who participated in the capture of Jerusalem
H5021.detail: Nebuzaradan is a chief of the eunuchs in the army of Nebuchadnezzar II. He appears alongside other Babylonian officers—Nebuzaradan (chief of the guards) and Nergal-Sharezer (chief of the magicians)—at the time when Jerusalem is conquered and the temple destroyed in 586 B.C. (Jeremiah 39:13). His name, which means "Nebo delivers me" (Nebo being a Babylonian deity), reflects the religious beliefs of Babylon.
H5021.origine: The name is of Babylonian origin, composed of two elements: Nebo, the god of wisdom and writing in Babylonian mythology, and a verb meaning "to deliver." This onomastic structure was common among the Babylonians, who incorporated the names of their gods into proper names to invoke their protection.
H5021.emploi: Nebuzaradan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 39:13, during the fall of Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar II. He is presented as one of the high military and administrative officials of the Babylonian empire, notably in charge of managing the eunuchs. His appearance in this historical account shows the personal involvement of high royal officers in the conquest and occupation of Jerusalem.

sens: Owner of a vineyard in Jezreel during the reign of Ahab
H5022.detail: Naboth is a man from the city of Jezreel who possesses a hereditary vineyard next to the palace of King Ahab of Samaria. The king covets this vineyard, but Naboth refuses to sell or exchange it, as it is the inheritance of his fathers (1 Kings 21:3-4). Ahab becomes sad and angry. His wife Jezebel decides to act secretly: she writes letters in Ahab's name to the elders of the city, ordering them to accuse Naboth of false testimony of blasphemy against God and the king. Two wicked men publicly denounce him, and Naboth is dragged out of the city and stoned (1 Kings 21:8-13). His death allows Ahab to seize his vineyard, thus fulfilling the crime he coveted. This is a blatant act of injustice that provokes the anger of the prophet Elijah and brings God's condemnation upon Ahab.
H5022.origine: The name Naboth literally means "fruits" in Hebrew. It is a meaningful name: a man whose name evokes fertility and harvest, but who will be dispossessed of his property through covetousness and deceit. His story remains famous in the Old Testament as an example of royal injustice and the cost of fidelity to family heritage in the face of tyranny.
H5022.emploi: Naboth is mentioned about 18 times in Scripture, almost exclusively in the account of 1 Kings 21. He also appears briefly in 2 Kings 9 when Jehu meets the kings Joram and Ahaziah in the field of Naboth, the place where his injustice was committed. The story of Naboth plays a central role in the judgment of Ahab: it illustrates the moral corruption of the king and the court, the manipulation of judicial institutions, and the cost of refusing to yield to royal covetousness. His name becomes synonymous with victim innocence and usurped rights.
H5022.portee: The account of Naboth teaches the Christian reader that covetousness and abuse of power trigger God's judgment, and that one should never sacrifice justice and family loyalty to acquire wealth. Naboth, though defeated and dead, remains morally victorious: he does not yield and preserves the honor of his heritage. His example speaks to all who suffer injustice: God sees, judges, and defends the innocent, even long after the events.

sens: Good, valuable object given as a reward or gratification
Payment or reward promised for a service rendered
H5023.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a material good, a valuable object offered as a gratification. In Daniel 2:6, King Nebuchadnezzar promises the diviner who interprets his dream precious gifts and great honors — these are presents, concrete rewards.
2. More broadly, it is a remuneration or payment intended to reward a service. When Daniel refuses in Daniel 5:17 the presents from King Belshazzar for the interpretation, he shows that this present is a form of salary or gratification for the work done.
H5023.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of giving or rewarding. It describes a present in the sense of a good given in exchange for a service, rather than a simple free gift. It is an administrative and royal term, common in ancient court contexts where kings reward those who serve them.
H5023.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the prophet Daniel, in chapter 2 and chapter 5. In these two passages, it refers to rewards promised or offered by Babylonian kings (Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar) in exchange for the interpretation of mysteries. The context is always that of a promised remuneration for an extraordinary service rendered to the king. It is an administrative term from ancient royal courts.
H5023.portee: These two accounts show that Daniel, although he has the power to serve kings by deciphering their mysteries, refuses earthly rewards. This illustrates his spiritual integrity and his conviction that his strength comes from God, not from worldly wealth or honor. The Christian can see a lesson about priorities: some loyalties cannot be bought.

sens: To bark like a dog
Figuratively, to cry out or alert, as a guard dog would
H5024.detail:
1. The verb literally denotes the bark of a dog, the characteristic sound it makes. It is the Hebrew word used to express this natural sound of the animal that barks.
2. The Bible uses this word figuratively to describe a failure: the mute dogs of the prophet (Isaiah 56:10) are an image of the guardians who do not sound the alarm, who do not fulfill their duty as watchmen. A dog must bark to warn; if it does not, it betrays its function. The text emphasizes that these blind guardians are "unable to bark": they do not play their role as sentinels.
H5024.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that imitates the bark of a dog. It is a descriptive word, rooted in the observation of nature. In biblical Hebrew, it expresses a specific sound: that produced by the animal when it watches or defends its territory. The image of the barking dog is naturally linked to vigilance and warning.
H5024.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 56:10. The prophet compares the religious leaders of Israel to guard dogs who do not fulfill their function. Instead of alerting the people and leading them toward justice and holiness, they remain mute and asleep. The context is one of severe criticism: the moral failure of Israel's shepherds, who should watch over the flock but do not. The use of the word "bark" reinforces the irony by comparing the guardians to beasts that are supposed to be vigilant.
H5024.portee: This word reminds the reader of the importance of spiritual vigilance. Religious and pastoral leaders are entrusted with a responsibility: to proclaim the truth, warn of danger, and call the people to justice. Remaining silent in the face of evil is to betray this mission. For the Christian, this invites not to passively accept moral indifference among those who have charge of souls, and not to be silent oneself in the face of injustice.

sens: Warrior of the tribe of Manasseh who conquered the city of Kenath during the entry into the Promised Land
Region of Gilead including Kenath and its surrounding villages, named after this warrior
H5025G.detail:
1. Nobach is a warrior belonging to the tribe of Manasseh. During the conquest of the territory east of the Jordan, he seizes the city of Kenath and the surrounding villages (Numbers 32:42). This is an act of military possession: Nobach acts as a conquistador, marking his victory by giving his own name to the conquered region.
2. Nobach also designates the region itself, this portion of Gilead that the warrior conquered and renamed after himself. It included the city of Kenath and its dependencies. This region retains this name in the account, although later it regains its original identity.
H5025G.origine: The name "Nobach" means "barking" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a quality of the warrior or simply an inherited nickname. The warrior bears this name and transmits it to the geographical conquest he accomplishes — a common practice in ancient Israel, where giving one's name to a city was a way to claim possession and leave a memorial for one's descendants.
H5025G.emploi: Nobach appears only once in the Old Testament, in Numbers 32:42, at the time of the division of territories east of the Jordan. At the end of the forty years in the desert, the Manassites occupy the mountainous region of Gilead. Nobach stands out by conquering Kenath and its villages, and he imposes his name on these lands. The text tells us nothing else about him: neither his origins, nor his descendants, nor his later exploits. It is a moment of foundation: a warrior marks history by his conquest, and his name becomes that of the place he took.

sens: Region of Gilead in the Land of Israel
Group of cities including Kenath and its villages
Name given by the conqueror of the region
H5025H.detail: 1. Nobach was a region located in Gilead, east of the Jordan, situated between the lands of Israel and the Arabian desert. 2. This region was made up of several cities including Kenath and its surrounding villages, making it a well-defined and populated territory. 3. The name "Nobach" literally means "barking" and was given to this region by its conqueror, which was a common practice among the Hebrews to name places after their conqueror.
H5025H.origine: The name Nobach comes from a root meaning "to bark" or "to cry out," perhaps evoking a war cry or a sound signal from the conqueror. Nobach is another name for the region also called Kenath (קְנָת). This dual name reflects how a region could retain its original identity while bearing the name of its conqueror. The region is mentioned in the context of the conquests of the Israelite tribes in the Promised Land.
H5025H.emploi: Nobach appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 8:11, during Gideon's pursuit of Midian. The text mentions Nobach as a geographical landmark on Gideon's route, alongside Jogbeha. This region was well-known and significant enough to serve as a reference point in accounts of war and conquest. It represents a part of the Israelite territory located east of the Jordan, in the area of Gilead.

sens: pagan deity worshiped by the Avvites
H5026.detail: Nibchaz is the name of an idol worshiped by the Avvites, a people who were settled in Samaria by the Assyrian king Shalmaneser after the deportation of the Israelites from the northern kingdom. The name means "the one who barks," and the idol took the form of a dog. The Avvites made Nibchaz and Tartak (2 Kings 17:31), along with other peoples who imported worship of other gods. This is one example among many of the multiplicity of idolatrous cults practiced in Samaria at that time.
H5026.origine: The name Nibchaz comes from a Semitic root meaning "to bark" or "to growl," which emphasizes the representation of the idol in the form of a dog. It is a name foreign to the Hebrew world, typical of the peoples of Mesopotamia and the Levant who were deported to Samaria by the Assyrians.
H5026.emploi: Nibchaz is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 17:31. This passage recalls how, after the fall of the kingdom of Israel in 722 B.C., the Assyrian Shalmaneser populated the region of Samaria with peoples of various origins. Each of these peoples introduced their own gods: the Avvites brought Nibchaz and Tartak, the Sepharvites brought Adrammelech and Anammelech. This biblical picture illustrates the religious mixing that marked Samaria after the captivity of the northern kingdom, and testifies to the multiplicity of idolatries that the people of God might have adopted.
H5026.portee: This passage helps the reader understand how idolatry took root in the Holy Land after the deportation: not only through the gradual perversion of the worship of the true God, but also through the massive importation of foreign religions. It underscores the importance of the commandment against false gods and shows how widespread idol worship was in the ancient world.

sens: To turn the eyes toward something or someone to see it
To pay attention to, to consider with interest or concern
To observe carefully, to examine
To have regard for, to esteem
To be careful of, to take heed to
To notice, to recognize by sight
H5027.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply to direct one's gaze toward an object or person: to turn the eyes to see. In Genesis 15:5, God says to Abraham: "Look toward the heavens, and count the stars," a direct invitation to lift his eyes and observe. In 1 Samuel 24:9, Saul "looked behind him," a physical movement of the eyes.

2. To look can mean to pay attention to something with a particular intention, to show interest or concern. In Isaiah 22:11, the people are reproached for not "looking to the one who planned these things," meaning they did not consider or take into account God and His work.

3. In some contexts, looking expresses careful observation or inspection: examining to know, understand, or judge. Psalms 33:13 says: "From heaven, the Lord looks," suggesting complete and vigilant knowledge.

4. To look can also mean to have regard, esteem, or kindness toward someone. In Psalms 10:14, the psalmist asks God to look, meaning to grant him attention and protection.

5. The verb also expresses the action of paying attention to, taking heed to something as a warning or teaching. In Proverbs 4:25, it is recommended to "look straight ahead," meaning to remain attentive and vigilant.

6. Finally, to look can simply mean to observe or notice a fact: to recognize by sight what is happening or exists. In Lamentations 1:12, there is an invitation to "look and see if there is any pain like mine."
H5027.origine: This Hebrew root comes from a primary image: to turn the eyes toward an object. It belongs to the family of verbs of visual perception, alongside words like "to see" (which covers a broader perception) and "to perceive." The Hebrew verb נָבַט is conjugated here in the Piel (intensive form) and Hiphil (causative form), which enriches the meaning: the Piel emphasizes the action of looking, while the Hiphil can give "to look" a nuance of causing to look, to show by looking, or to cause an action as a result of a look.
H5027.emploi: This verb appears 67 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms, the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs), and the prophets (Isaiah, Lamentations). It expresses both a simple act (turning the eyes) and an act loaded with spiritual meaning: to look at God is to recognize Him and trust Him; to look at creation is to admire it; to look at one's neighbor is to care for them. In Psalms 104:32, God's gaze upon the earth causes it to tremble: it is a power. In Isaiah 63:15 and 64:8, the people plead with God to "look" from heaven, meaning to come down to their aid. In Lamentations, the word returns to express the urgent need to be seen and helped by God. The verb nuances its meaning according to the context: it can be an ordinary gesture of life (looking back), a vigilant attention (God who sees everything), or a moral action (to look, meaning to recognize and act).
H5027.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb reminds us that the gaze is never neutral. To look at God is to welcome Him and obey Him; to be looked at by God is to be known, loved, and called to change. It also invites us to examine our own gazes: do we see the poor, the suffering, those who are forgotten? The verb teaches that God sees everything, that He does not turn His eyes away from evil or from the tears of His children.

sens: Man of the kingdom of Israel during the time of the united monarchy
Father of Jeroboam I
Ephraimite from Zeredah
Dynastic ancestor whose name becomes synonymous with religious schism
H5028.detail:
1. Nebath is a man living during the time of the united monarchy of Israel, an Ephraimite from Zeredah. He first appears as the father of the future king Jeroboam (1 Kings 11:26).
2. His historical significance lies in the fact that he is the father of Jeroboam I, who became king of the Northern Kingdom after the political and religious schism that divided Israel at the death of Solomon (1 Kings 12:2).
3. His name becomes a generational reference: the kings who followed him in the Northern Kingdom are described as having imitated "the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebath," which means they maintained the idolatrous worship established at Bethel and Dan (2 Kings 13:2; 15:18; 22:53).
4. The expression "son of Nebath" functions as a moral label summarizing the schism and religious apostasy: it reminds us that any king who reproduces the sins of Jeroboam perpetuates the break with the true worship of the God of Israel that occurred under this first dynasty of the North (2 Kings 17:21).
H5028.origine: The name Nebath literally means "aspect" or "appearance" in Hebrew. Little known before his son, Nebath enters biblical history through the notoriety of Jeroboam, of whom he is the father. His patronymic becomes inextricably linked to the great religious schism of Israel: the expression "son of Nebath" acquires a symbolic significance far beyond the simple genealogical link.
H5028.emploi: Nebath appears 25 times in the Bible, exclusively in the books of Kings and Chronicles, always in the formula "Jeroboam, son of Nebath." He never appears alone but always to identify Jeroboam and, by extension, to characterize all the kings of the North who followed. This formula particularly recurs in the condemnatory formulas of the kings: almost all the rulers of the Northern Kingdom are described as having "done what was evil in the sight of the Lord" and "not having abandoned the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebath" (1 Kings 16:26; 2 Kings 3:3; 13:11; 14:24). Even the great king Josiah, reformer of the South, demolished the high places erected by Jeroboam, son of Nebath (2 Kings 23:15). The name thus functions as a historical and moral marker: it marks the origin point of the systematic idolatry of the Northern Kingdom.
H5028.portee: For the Christian reader, Nebath embodies the generational anchor of sin: his son Jeroboam introduced the worship of golden calves, and for centuries, each king of the North is measured by this standard. It is a reminder that the choices of one generation can mark the history of an entire people. The repeated mention of "Jeroboam, son of Nebath" teaches us that apostasy is never neutral: it creates a trajectory that, unless repented, perpetuates itself. At the same time, it is an invitation to break with the twisted paths: Josiah had the courage to destroy the sinful legacy of Nebath.

sens: one who speaks on behalf of God
one who conveys a divine message
one who communicates God's will to the people
H5029.detail: 1. The prophet is a man chosen by God to speak in His name to the people. He does not invent his words: he receives them from God and reports them faithfully. In the book of Ezra, Haggai and Zechariah are called "prophets" because they communicated God's will to the people, notably the command to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 5:1). 2. The prophet assists and accompanies the people by reminding them of God's intentions. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah "assisted" those who were building the temple, meaning they strengthened them by telling them that God approved and guided their actions (Ezra 5:2). 3. The prophecies of the prophet are a source of authority and certainty: they express what God truly wants. When the temple was completed, the Bible notes that this work was done "according to the prophecies of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah" (Ezra 6:14), showing that the words of the prophets gave meaning and legitimacy to the actions of the people.
H5029.origine: The Aramaic word נְבִיא comes from the same root as the Hebrew נָבִיא (prophet, H5030). This root refers to the image of one who speaks forth, who announces, who proclaims. A prophet is literally someone who speaks for another, or who speaks in advance of what is to come. The term is borrowed from Hebrew and used in Aramaic in the parts of the book of Ezra written in that language.
H5029.emploi: This word appears three times in the book of Ezra, all in Aramaic (chapters 5 and 6), always to designate prophetic figures from the time of the return from exile. Haggai and Zechariah, the two major prophets of this period, are the only ones mentioned by this term in these passages. Their role is twofold: on one hand, they communicate God's orders and encouragements regarding the reconstruction of the temple; on the other hand, they serve as divine endorsement to the leaders of the people (Zerubbabel and Joshua) by attesting that this work pleases God. The context shows that the prophet is essentially the one through whom God's will passes in the decisive moments of the history of the people.
H5029.portee: Understanding what a prophet is helps the reader to respect the word of God reported in the Bible. The prophets did not speak on their own initiative, but as spokespersons for God; their words therefore had absolute authority. This is why the Christian faith places such importance on prophetic writings: they testify to how God has guided His people and what He wants for us.

sens: One who speaks in the name of God, who receives and transmits His word
One who announces the future according to divine revelation
One who is a false prophet who deceives by claiming to speak for God
One who performs this function in worship or before kings
One who sees and understands the will of God
H5030.detail:
1. The prophet is fundamentally a spokesperson, one to whom God entrusts His words to convey to the people. He is a man called and inspired, like Abraham, whom God designates as a "prophet" to intercede (Genesis 20:7). The prophet speaks on behalf of God, with divine authority behind his words.

2. The prophet announces what is to come, for he sees beyond the present through divine revelation. People come to consult the prophets to know the will of the Lord and what He has in store (Ezekiel 7:26: "They seek visions from the prophets").

3. The false prophet is one who speaks claiming to come from God, but who lies and misleads the people. The Bible warns against these impostors who "prophesy" lies (Jeremiah 27:16: "Do not listen to the words of your prophets who prophesy to you... For it is a lie that they prophesy to you").

4. The prophet can also be a counselor to kings, like Isaiah to Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:1), or a healer and intercessor endowed with extraordinary powers.
H5030.origine: The Hebrew word nabî (נָבִיא) likely comes from a root meaning "to call" or "to announce." It refers to one who is called by God to announce. In ancient Hebrew, the term "seer" (ro'eh) is also used to designate the prophet, emphasizing that he "sees" hidden things. The word retains this dual dimension: to speak and to see, to announce and to reveal.
H5030.emploi: The word "prophet" appears 310 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical books (Samuel, Kings) and among the prophets themselves (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). In the time of Samuel, the prophets formed groups and lived in community (1 Samuel 10:5, 10:10). Under the kings, they played a political and religious role: they advised the kings (2 Samuel 7:2), rebuked them when they strayed from God (Jeremiah 27:16), and announced the future in the name of the Lord (1 Kings 16:12).
