The text also distinguishes false prophets, who proliferate in times of crisis and deceive the people (1 Kings 22:6-23, Jeremiah 27:16). The role of the prophet culminates in the Old Testament: Moses himself is presented as the unmatched model of the prophet (Deuteronomy 34:10).
H5030.portee: Understanding what a prophet is helps to grasp how God speaks to the people of the Old Testament: not first through written words, but through inspired men, living voices that convey His will. It also highlights the importance of discerning the true from the false, listening to those who truly speak on behalf of God, and rejecting impostors. For the Christian, this sheds light on how God progressively revealed Himself, culminating in sending Jesus, who is presented in continuity with the prophetic function.

sens: woman endowed with the gift of prophecy, who speaks in the name of God
woman inspired to sing and celebrate God
woman consulted to receive a word from God
woman who falsely claims to be a prophet
H5031.detail:
1. A prophetess is a woman chosen by God to speak in His name and convey His message to the people. Miriam, sister of Aaron, was a prophetess during the Exodus: she did not receive long messages like her brother Moses, but she possessed the inspired gift of singing and leading the praise of the people (Exodus 15:20).
2. Deborah was a prophetess and also a judge in Israel, which shows that this gift could be exercised in governance and counsel (Judges 4:4). She guided the people by the word that God gave her.
3. Huldah was a prophetess who was consulted like an oracle: when King Josiah wanted to know the will of God, he sent his ministers to her to receive her word (2 Kings 22:14, 2 Chronicles 34:22).
4. Noadiah was a false prophetess: she claimed to speak on behalf of God, but her message was deceitful and contrary to His will (Nehemiah 6:14).
H5031.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to speak" or "to bubble" (to produce a prophetic word). It is the feminine form of "prophet" (נְבִיא, nebi). In the prophetic tradition of Israel, this gift of speaking in the name of God was recognized among certain women as well as men, although it is less documented. The prophetess was one to whom God revealed His will so that she could communicate it.
H5031.emploi: This word appears six times in the Bible, always in the singular and referring to a particular woman. It is first encountered in the time of Moses (Miriam), then in the time of the judges (Deborah), and later in the time of the kings (Huldah during the time of Josiah). Each usage shows a different role: Miriam expresses prophetic praise, Deborah exercises governance, and Huldah gives consulted oracles. The word also designates a false prophetess (Noadiah). Isaiah's wife is called a prophetess, perhaps because she participated in her husband's prophetic gift or because she herself was endowed with such a gift.
H5031.portee: The presence of prophetesses in the history of Israel shows that God has never limited His gift of prophecy to men alone: He has spoken through women to guide, instruct, and comfort His people. This reminds us that the Spirit of God blows where He wills, without distinction. It is also a call to discern between the true and the false prophet: the lie of Noadiah contrasts with the faithfulness of Huldah, inviting us to listen wisely.

sens: firstborn son of Ishmael
Arab people descended from Nebajoth, the Nabataeans
Region or territory associated with the Arab peoples of the Middle East
H5032.detail:
1. Nebajoth is the firstborn son of Ishmael, who is himself the son of Abraham. He is mentioned in the genealogy of Ishmael at the time when Abraham awaits the fulfillment of God's promises. He is an ancestor of several Arab peoples who will occupy the desert regions of the Middle East.

2. By extension, Nebajoth designates the people and nation that descended from this son of Ishmael. This people is later historically known as the Nabataeans, an Arab people who established a great commercial kingdom with its capital at Petra. In Isaiah 60:7, the prophet speaks of the flocks and rams of Nebajoth, which signifies the pastoral wealth of this Arab people.

3. The name may also evoke the territory or region where these Arab peoples lived, in the desert and high plateaus of the Middle East.
H5032.origine: The name Nebajoth literally means "heights" in Hebrew, which likely reflects the geography of the lands where this people settled. Ishmael, the father of Nebajoth, is the son of Abraham and the Egyptian servant Hagar. Nebajoth is his firstborn and the leader of his descendants. The name appears in the genealogical list of Ishmael, and his brothers include Kedar and other ancestors of Arab peoples.
H5032.emploi: Nebajoth appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in genealogical contexts. It is first mentioned in Genesis 25:13 as the firstborn of Ishmael. The name reappears in Genesis 28:9 and 36:3, where he is mentioned as the brother of Mahalath, whom the patriarchs marry. In 1 Chronicles 1:29, the genealogy of Ishmael is repeated. The most significant prophetic usage is found in Isaiah 60:7, where the prophet announces that the flocks of Kedar and the rams of Nebajoth will be offered in sacrifice on the altar of God, symbolizing the conversion of the Arab peoples and their adherence to the God of Israel.
H5032.portee: Nebajoth represents in Scripture the promise that the descendants of Ishmael and the Arab peoples will ultimately be included in God's plan of salvation. By this name, the Bible acknowledges that the Arabs are not forgotten by God, but included in His redemptive project for all peoples. Isaiah 60:7 offers a vision of hope: this people, long spiritually distant, will bring their wealth and worship to the true God.

sens: Underground place where water springs up
Point of origin or departure
H5033.detail: 1. The word literally designates the water source, the place where water naturally emerges from the ground or rock. In Job 38:16, God asks Job if he has penetrated to the sources of the sea, meaning the mysterious depths from which water springs, in the ancient image of the world where water comes from underground reservoirs. 2. By extension, the word evokes the origin or starting point of something, as a source provides the beginning of a river's course.
H5033.origine: The Hebrew word nevekh comes from a root that expresses the idea of springing forth or emerging. It literally designates the place from which water springs. This image of the source as a point of origin is found in many ancient Near Eastern languages.
H5033.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 38:16. It is found in God's discourse questioning Job about the mysteries of creation and the structure of the world. The cosmological context shows that the word is used to designate the underground sources of water, in accordance with the ancient vision of a universe where deep waters feed the visible seas and rivers.
H5033.portee: This mention of the hidden sources of the sea invites the believer to recognize that behind visible realities lie mysterious origins known and controlled only by God. It calls for humility in the face of the secrets of creation and the divine wisdom that surpasses our understanding.

sens: To be devoid of sense, to lack discernment
To treat someone with contempt or disdain
To dishonor, to bring into dishonor
To lower or degrade someone in consideration
H5034A.detail:
1. In its primary sense, the word describes a form of folly or lack of judgment: it is to lose reason, to act without thinking. When Israel forsakes God and "despises the Rock of his salvation" (Deuteronomy 32:15), it commits monumental folly, rejecting the one who created it with disdain.
2. To treat someone with contempt means to regard them as unworthy, to publicly belittle them. In Micah 7:6, the son "outrages" his father: he treats him disrespectfully, shaming him before all.
3. To dishonor someone means to attack their honor, their dignity. Jeremiah pleads: "For your name's sake, do not despise, do not dishonor the throne of your glory" (Jeremiah 14:21) — he asks God to preserve his honor and that of his people.
4. To degrade means to reduce someone to the lowest state, to publicly shame them. The prophet Nahum announces: "I will degrade you, and I will make you a spectacle" (Nahum 3:6) — a total humiliation.
H5034A.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to be empty, to be devoid." The same family is found in Hebrew with words describing foolishness or futility. The initial image is that of a person emptied of reason, becoming hollow, foolish. From this come the senses of treating as a fool, thus with contempt, and of reducing someone to nothingness, to shame.
H5034A.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the Old Testament, mainly at moments when God or the people act with derision or dishonor. In Deuteronomy 32:15, it is Israel that "despises" God in its unfaithfulness. In Proverbs 30:32, it is pride that leads to acts of folly. Jeremiah and Nahum use it to describe dishonor and degradation: either God is asked not to dishonor his throne, or he threatens to bring down his enemies. In Micah 7:6, the son outrages the father. The word expresses each time a rupture of respect, a serious violation of the due that one owes to someone or to God.
H5034A.portee: This word highlights the gravity of contempt and dishonor in biblical faith. When Israel despises God, it is not a mere mistake: it is folly that leads to its own ruin. Conversely, degrading someone is to commit a profoundly inhumane act. The believer learns that respect — towards God and towards others — is not a moral luxury, but a vital requirement.

sens: To wilt, fall, collapse physically
To lose strength, energy, to exhaust oneself
To dry up, to wither, to lose luster
To disappear, perish, cease to be
H5034B.detail:
1. The primary sense is that of a fall or collapse: something solid crumbles or collapses. Job 14:18 illustrates this well: "The mountain crumbles and perishes."
2. By extension, the word describes the exhaustion of strength and energy. In Exodus 18:18, Moses will "exhaust" himself if he continues to judge all the people alone — the verb describes a fatigue that consumes.
3. The most common sense in the Bible is that of the wilting of plants: they dry up, wither, lose their luster. Isaiah 1:30 speaks of a terebinth with "withered" foliage, and Isaiah 28:1 of a flower that is "faded."
4. These three images (fall, exhaustion, wilting) converge on the idea of a gradual disappearance or destruction: Isaiah 34:4 describes the leaves of the vine and fig tree that "fall" — life departs.
H5034B.origine: The Hebrew verb נָבֵל (navel) comes from a root that fundamentally evokes collapse and fall. In Hebrew, we find the noun נָבֵל (nevel), which designates a vessel, a container that collapses or falls. The central image is that of something losing its tension, rigidity, vigor — like a plant that shrivels or skin that withers. The word describes both the physical reality (the collapse of a mountain) and the moral and spiritual image (the exhaustion of strength).
H5034B.emploi: This verb appears 16 times in the Bible, mainly in the Psalms and by the prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah. It first applies to the plant world: grass that withers (Psalms 37:2, Isaiah 40:7), the crown flower of Ephraim that dehydrates (Isaiah 28:1, 28:4). It also describes natural disasters: a mountain that collapses (Job 14:18), the heavens dissolving (Isaiah 34:4). When applied to people, it depicts physical exhaustion (Exodus 18:18) or the discouragement of enemies (Psalms 18:46). Finally, in an eschatological context, it symbolizes the ruin of human works and the vanity of what does not endure: leaves fall, kingdoms collapse, everything that is not of the Lord perishes.
H5034B.portee: This word speaks to the believer about the fragility of all that is earthly and detached from God. The Bible uses it to describe both the weariness of our physical strength — a call not to exhaust ourselves through pride — and the inevitable death of all that does not take root in God. But the context of the Psalms adds hope: the one who is rooted in God will not wither (Psalms 1:3), while his enemies will collapse. It is an invitation to seek our stability not in ourselves or in this world, but in the one who alone endures.

sens: Leather container used to hold liquids
Clay vase or pot
Poetic image of the capacity to contain
H5035A.detail:
1. The 'outre' is a flexible container, usually made from sewn animal skin, used to transport and preserve liquids — especially wine and water. It is a common object in everyday Israelite life: Abigail prepares two filled with wine to appease David (1 Samuel 25:18), and a man can carry one on the road (1 Samuel 10:3).
2. The word also refers to a vase or pot made of clay, a rigid container as opposed to the soft skin. These vases served as household utensils for storage (Isaiah 22:24).
3. In a more poetic and figurative usage, the 'outre' represents that which contains, that which can hold or pour: Job speaks of the 'outres of the heavens' to evoke the clouds that pour rain (Job 38:37), an image of celestial reservoirs full of water.
H5035A.origine: The Hebrew word נֵ֫בֶל (nébel) likely comes from a root that evokes the idea of 'inflating' or 'filling up', which perfectly suits a wineskin filled with liquid. This image of what contains and fills also appears in passages where the word takes on a figurative tone, as in Job where the clouds are seen as outres pouring their rain.
H5035A.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (1 and 2 Samuel) and in poetic texts (Job, Jeremiah). In the narratives, it is always a concrete object of domestic life: it is brought on journeys (1 Samuel 10:3), offered as a gift (1 Samuel 25:18), filled with wine (2 Samuel 16:1). In the poetic passages (Job 38:37), the word becomes an image: the 'outres of the heavens' symbolize rain. Jeremiah uses it in a symbolic act that plays on the double meaning of the word: breaking an outre (Jeremiah 13:12).
H5035A.portee: For the Christian reader, the 'outre' reminds us that the Bible speaks the language of simple and concrete things in everyday life. It also invites us to meditate on the biblical image of the container: we are 'vessels' in God's hands, capable of receiving and pouring out what He entrusts to us. The image of the heavenly outres in Job opens the heavens as a generous source of water and life.

sens: Stringed instrument, elongated in shape, used in orchestras and religious celebrations in Israel
Symbol of joy, praise, and music in the worship of the Lord
H5035B.detail:
1. The lute is a stringed musical instrument that is plucked with the fingers to produce sounds. The Bible always mentions it alongside other instruments like the harp, flute, or cymbals, particularly during major religious festivals. When David brings the ark to Jerusalem, the people 'played the harp, the lute, and the cymbals' to honor God (1 Chronicles 13:8).
2. Figuratively, the lute represents joy and praise directed to God. In the Psalms, the poet calls his own lute to awaken to praise the Lord: 'Awake, my lute and harp! I will awaken the dawn' (Psalms 57:9), transforming the instrument into a symbol of his exultant soul.
H5035B.origine: The Hebrew word nébel comes from a root meaning 'to inflate' or 'to be hollow', which aptly describes the rounded and hollow shape of the instrument. In Hebrew, there is also the verb 'nabel' (to pour, to spread), which can evoke the resonance of sound that springs from this hollow instrument. The word belongs to the family of terms designating stringed instruments characteristic of ancient Middle Eastern music.
H5035B.emploi: The lute appears 27 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in musical cultic or celebratory contexts. It is mentioned mainly in Chronicles (where David uses it to accompany worship) and in the Psalms (where it becomes a poetic image of praise). It is always a noble instrument, never trivial: it is found during the ascent of the ark (1 Chronicles 13:8), during the dedication festivals of the temple (2 Chronicles 5:12), and in hymns of gratitude. Isaiah ironically mentions it among the wealthy who are indifferent (Isaiah 5:12) and Amos condemns it when it accompanies idolatry (Amos 5:23).
H5035B.portee: The lute teaches us that true joy is a response to the presence of God. It is an instrument for celebration, for praise, to express a heart filled with gratitude. When the Bible contrasts it with debauchery (in Isaiah), it reminds us that music itself is neither good nor bad: it all depends on the heart that plays it and the God it honors.

sens: Lacking wisdom and understanding
Acting without reflection or fear of God
Criminal, infamous, vile in conduct
One who obstinately rejects divine wisdom
H5036.detail:
1. The fool is primarily one who lacks sense, natural judgment. In Deuteronomy 32:6, Moses reproaches the people for being a 'foolish people' — they have not recognized that the Lord is their creator and father, despite His evident blessings. It is a lack of basic intelligence, a blindness to realities.
2. The fool acts without reflection and without fear of God. He utters folly (Isaiah 32:6) and gives his heart to evil; he speaks and acts impulsively, forgetting the consequences. In Psalms 14:1, the fool 'says in his heart: There is no God' — not out of sincere ignorance, but out of a kind of light and stupid defiance.
3. The word also designates the infamous or vile man, whose acts are ignoble. In 2 Samuel 13:13, Tamar uses this word for a shameful and criminal act against a woman. The fool here is no longer just foolish; he is despicable.
4. Finally, the fool is one who deliberately rejects wisdom and God's order. The false prophets are fools (Ezekiel 13:3) who speak without having received the word of the Lord. It is a form of unconscious rebellion against God.
H5036.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of 'emptiness' or 'hollowness' — the fool is one whose head is empty of sense, reflection, and divine fear. This image of an inner emptiness distinguishes the fool from the simply ignorant: it is a choice or habit of not thinking. The word also has a moral nuance — the fool is not just clumsy, he is morally inferior or guilty.
H5036.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms and Proverbs, where biblical wisdom repeatedly addresses it. Moses uses it to describe rebellious Israel (Deuteronomy 32:6, 32:21); the Psalmists apply it to those who deny God or despise His name (Psalms 14:1, 74:18); the wise in Proverbs sound it out to family heads to warn them against foolish children (Proverbs 17:21). The prophets use it to denounce the evil committed — wickedness, impiety, falsehood — and the false prophets who deceive the people. The word oscillates between intellectual deficiency and moral guilt: a fool is not so because he is weak-minded, but because he chooses to live far from God and His order.
H5036.portee: Recognizing that the Bible qualifies as foolish one who lives without God or without fear of God helps the reader grasp that true intelligence is not about degrees or outward success, but the awareness that there is a divine authority above us. The fool is one who, even if intellectually intelligent, refuses this reality. This word calls for humility and the fear of the Lord as the beginning of wisdom.

sens: Man from Carmel during the united monarchy
Husband of Abigail
The one who insulted David's messengers
Died of shock upon learning of the danger he had faced
H5037.detail:
1. Nabal is a wealthy man living in Carmel during the time of King David, owner of large flocks of sheep and goats. His name means "fool" in Hebrew, which perfectly corresponds to his character: Scripture describes him as "harsh and evil in his deeds" (1 Samuel 25:3).

2. He is the husband of Abigail, a sensible and beautiful woman, who stands in stark contrast to her husband with her intelligence and wisdom (1 Samuel 25:3).

3. When David's servants came to him courteously asking for help, Nabal insulted them and contemptuously refused, disregarding the one who had protected him. David, furious, decided to avenge this humiliation by force (1 Samuel 25:9-11).

4. Abigail, without saying anything to her husband, went to appease David with gifts. When she reported to Nabal what had happened, he had a stroke, and ten days later the Lord struck him, and he died, taking his wealth but not his life (1 Samuel 25:37-38).
H5037.origine: The Hebrew name נָבָל (nabal) literally means "fool" or "insensate." It comes from a root that expresses the idea of a vile, despicable person, lacking discernment. This name is not chosen randomly by the biblical narrator: it reveals the heart of the one who bears it. In 1 Samuel 25:25, Abigail herself explains that "Nabal" corresponds to his nature: "He lives up to his name, for Nabal means folly, and folly is with him."
H5037.emploi: Nabal appears eighteen times in the Bible, exclusively in the narratives of the Davidic cycle (1 Samuel 25-30 and 2 Samuel 2-3). The most important text is 1 Samuel 25, which details the incident with David: Nabal's refusal to help David, who had protected his shepherds, the mediation of his wife Abigail, and his sudden death. After his death, he is still mentioned as Abigail's husband, who became one of David's wives (1 Samuel 30:5; 2 Samuel 2:2). Nabal illustrates the man who despises God's servant and refuses good, in contrast to Abigail, who recognizes God's plan. His story shows how God protects those who seek Him.
H5037.portee: The story of Nabal and Abigail teaches that wealth and power mean nothing without wisdom and the fear of God. Nabal represents the foolish man who refuses to recognize those whom God has chosen, and upon whom divine judgment strikes pride. It also shows the value of a wise woman: Abigail saves her household from destruction by intervening with discernment. For the believer, this account is a call to recognize God's work even among those whom the world rejects, and not to confuse material wealth with true honor.

sens: the lifeless body of an animal or human
what remains of a living creature after its death
a corpse subject to decomposition
that which symbolizes death and curse
the biblical image of divine judgment on sin
H5038.detail:
1. A corpse is the inert body of an animal or person after death. In Leviticus 5:2, touching the corpse of a dead animal renders a person unclean: this is a physical, concrete reality that defiles anyone who comes into contact with it.
2. It is what remains of a living creature after the soul has departed, destined for decay. Leviticus 11:39 states that "anyone who touches its dead body will be unclean until evening," showing that the corpse is considered radically separated from life.
3. An abandoned body left to decompose, often exposed to birds and beasts. Jeremiah 7:33 announces: "The corpses of this people will be food for the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth," an image of ultimate dishonor.
4. The corpse becomes a symbol of curse and death under judgment. Deuteronomy 21:23 says that the hanged man "must not remain on the tree overnight," for "anyone who is hanged is under God's curse."
5. In Isaiah 26:19, "your dead will live, your corpses will rise," the word evokes the ultimate promise of resurrection, showing that even death does not have the final word in the face of God's power.
H5038.origine: The Hebrew word nevélah comes from a root that expresses the idea of withering or decay. It literally designates what has lost life and begins to decompose. This word is rooted in the Old Testament experience of purity laws: contact with corpses rendered one ritually unclean, and this principle structures a large part of the legislation in Leviticus. The word has no unique Greek equivalent but is rendered by different terms depending on the context.
H5038.emploi: The word appears 41 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, where it regulates ritual impurities. Leviticus 11 discusses it at length to distinguish clean animals from unclean ones and the rules of defilement. Deuteronomy 21:23 uses it in the context of capital punishment. It also appears in historical narratives: in 1 Kings 13, the lion guards the corpse of the disobedient prophet without devouring it, a miraculous sign from God. Jeremiah uses it to announce judgment: the corpses will remain unburied, a supreme outrage. In Isaiah 26:19, the word shifts towards hope: the corpses will rise at the resurrection. The meaning remains one of definitive death and defilement, except when resurrection redeems it.
H5038.portee: This word reminds the believer of the stark reality of death and the judgment that follows. The purity laws regarding the corpse teach that death has infected the world through sin, and that even contact with it requires purification. For the Christian, the image of the corpse left to the crows (Jeremiah) becomes a warning about the consequences of sin and rejection of God. But Isaiah 26:19 shifts the meaning: it announces that the risen Jesus has conquered death, and that our corpses will also rise. This is why the word carries the hope of resurrection for those who believe.

sens: shameful and scandalous action, contrary to morality
insensate folly that brings dishonor
act of immorality or profanation
that which violates the laws and norms of Israel
H5039.detail:
1. An infamy is primarily a scandalous, shameful action that provokes indignation: when Shechem lies with Dinah without being married to her, it is an "infamy" that incites the furious anger of Jacob's sons (Genesis 34:7). The word evokes a serious violation of propriety, an act that should never be done.
2. Infamy is also senseless folly, a stupid and disastrous action: one who commits an infamy acts without reason, without considering the shame they bring upon themselves and their community. In 1 Samuel 25:25, Nabal is described as a man "of infamous name," meaning he is known for his foolish acts.
3. Infamy often refers to sexual immorality or profane acts: violating a woman, committing unnatural acts, is to commit an infamy (Judges 19:23-24). It can also be a transgression of the covenant with the Lord (Joshua 7:15).
4. It is an act that dishonors all of Israel, attracting God's judgment upon the people: Gibeah has committed an infamy and must be punished (Judges 20:10). Infamy is never a private act: it affects the community of believers.
H5039.origine: The Hebrew word nevala comes from a root that expresses insensitivity, lack of heart and wisdom. It designates what is devoid of modesty and moral sense. The same root appears in other words for "fool" or "insensate." It is a word that carries the idea that committing an infamy is to act without intelligence, without respect for the order established by God.
H5039.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used primarily in narratives of serious sexual acts or moral violence: violation, immorality (Genesis 34:7, 2 Samuel 13:12), and also in contexts of covenant transgression or profanation (Joshua 7:15). The prophets use it to condemn the moral impiety of Judah (Isaiah 9:16, 32:6; Jeremiah 29:23). Each time, infamy is a serious act that provokes the indignation of the community and the judgment of God, never a simple mistake or a minor fault.
H5039.portee: Understanding what an infamy is in the eyes of the Bible is to grasp that God does not take lightly the violation of His moral order. An infamy is not a hidden fault: it sullies the entire community and calls for judgment. For the Christian, this word reminds us that certain acts are never acceptable, that they offend both God and the community of believers, and that they must be decisively avoided.

sens: Total absence of modesty and restraint in behavior or appearance
Conduct or speech that offends decency and morality
Nudity or shameful exposure of the body
H5040.detail:
1. The word denotes a complete absence of modesty, that virtue which naturally urges us to avoid anything that might offend. It is indecency in its most brutal form, without any restraint or respect. In Hosea 2:12, God threatens to uncover the "shame" of unfaithful Israel before its lovers: the image is one of public and humiliating exposure, where what should remain hidden is brought to light.
2. The word can also refer to impudent acts or words that hurt morality and dignity. It is the behavior of one who is unashamed of their actions and has no fear of judgment.
3. The term can refer to nudity or parts of the body that, by nature, should remain covered. This exposure is doubly shameful: it violates personal modesty and provokes shame in those who witness it.
H5040.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be empty" or "to be devoid." Indecency is thus a form of moral emptiness and deprivation: deprivation of modesty, deprivation of self-respect. It belongs to the same family as words expressing absence, deficiency, or insufficiency. It is therefore a strong concept: to have no indecency is to have the fullness of modesty and restraint.
H5040.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Hosea 2:12. God, speaking through the prophet, threatens to expose Israel's unfaithfulness: He will uncover its "shame" before its lovers. The context is that of divine judgment on Israel's unfaithfulness, which has prostituted itself by following other gods. The exposure of this shame is both a consequence of unfaithfulness and a public humiliation intended to bring the people to repentance.
H5040.portee: This word reminds the believer that modesty is not merely a social convention, but a virtue related to self-respect and respect for God. Indecency is its opposite: it reflects a total loss of the sense of what is right and proper. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to cultivate restraint in actions and words, not out of fear of shame, but out of respect for oneself and for the holiness that God expects from the believer.

sens: city of Benjamin reoccupied after the exile
H5041.detail: Neballath is a city that belonged to the tribe of Benjamin. After the return from exile, it was repopulated by the Israelites returning to their territory (Nehemiah 11:34).
H5041.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "hidden folly." The precise origin and ancient history of this place are not documented in the available biblical references.
H5041.emploi: Neballath appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:34, in the list of cities of Benjamin that the Benjaminites reoccupied after returning from the Babylonian exile. It is mentioned alongside other cities like Hadid and Zeboim.

sens: To flow, to pour out, or to overflow from a source
To come out of the mouth, in words or cries
To make known, express, proclaim publicly
To render abundant, to pour generously
H5042.detail:
1. The verb first describes a movement of fluid that flows or springs forth: water gushing from a source, a liquid bubbling or fermenting. It is the image of something that rises and comes out naturally, with force and abundance.
2. The Bible applies it to the word that comes from the mouth: the evil that the wicked cry out (Psalms 59:8), the words that cannot be restrained. It is as if the word were a torrent overflowing from the lips.
3. The word also takes on the meaning of "publishing" or "making known": publishing wisdom (Psalms 78:2), proclaiming the praise of the Lord (Psalms 119:171). To make a truth gush forth is to bring it to light, to make it audible and visible.
4. Finally, it can evoke abundance that overflows: the immense goodness of the Lord (Psalms 145:7) is so great that it comes forth from all sides, that it cannot be contained.
H5042.origine: The Hebrew verb נָבַע comes from a root that suggests bubbling and pouring out. The primary image is that of water boiling, fermenting, rising and coming out of itself. Related words in biblical Hebrew refer to this idea of flowing and coming out. The root evokes the naturalness of the movement: it is not forcing something, it is letting it flow from where it should flow.
H5042.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and Proverbs. It primarily denotes the flow of what comes out naturally: the gushing forth of evil from the lips of the wicked (Psalms 59:8). But it also applies to wise words or praise: one publishes ancient wisdom (Psalms 78:2), one proclaims the goodness of the Lord (Psalms 145:7). Proverbs uses it to show how wise words flow from one who has discernment (Proverbs 15:28: "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer"). The verb can also mean "to discourse" with assurance or arrogance (Psalms 94:4). Thus, the word follows the image of the flow: words or feelings that come from an inner source (the heart, the mouth) to the outside.
H5042.portee: This verb reminds us that our words come from what fills our hearts: they are not isolated acts, but the gushing forth of what we carry within. It invites the believer to fill their heart with the Word of God and His praise, so that what gushes forth from their mouth is not evil or arrogance, but the wisdom and glory of the Lord (Psalms 119:171).

sens: support portant une ou plusieurs lampes à huile
objet de lumière et de visibilité dans un palais royal
H5043.detail:
1. The chandelier is a support made of wood or metal where one or more oil lamps are placed to illuminate a room. It is a common household item in ancient Orient, distinct from the large seven-branched candelabrum of the Jewish temple. In Daniel 5:5, it is in front of this chandelier that the mysterious hand writes on the wall of Belshazzar's palace: the lamp that burns near the king is a silent witness to divine judgment.
2. The chandelier also symbolizes clarity and visible presence: the hand writes where the light shines, making the message readable and undeniable. This detail emphasizes the public and manifest nature of God's judgment.
H5043.origine: The Aramaic word nev.re.sah likely comes from a root indicating that which bears or supports. It is a common term for any utensil used to hold one or more oil lamps. The context of Daniel shows that it is an object of the royal palace, not the sacred furniture of the temple.
H5043.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 5:5. It refers to the chandelier of Belshazzar's palace where the king feasts. It is in the light of this chandelier that the mysterious hand writes the words of judgment on the wall: "Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin." The context emphasizes that the divine message is inscribed visibly and indubitably, close to the light, as if to guarantee that no one can ignore the judgment.
H5043.portee: This detail of the chandelier reminds us that God's judgment is not hidden or ambiguous: it manifests in the light, before all. In our lives, this invites us to seek clarity and truth rather than darkness, and to recognize that God speaks openly to those who have eyes to see.

sens: Ville ancienne de Judée, située dans le désert
H5044.detail: Nibschan is a small town in Judea mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Joshua lists the six towns in the desert of Judea (Joshua 15:62). The name literally means "soft soil" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking the clayey or low lands of this desert region. Nibschan was located in the arid area near the Dead Sea, alongside other towns like En-Gedi.
H5044.origine: The name Nibschan comes from the Hebrew נִבְשָׁן and means "soft soil" or "tender land," formed from a root describing a soft or marshy terrain. This type of topographical designation reflects the geological characteristics of the place: an area where the soil, despite the general dryness of the Judean desert, presented low or moist areas, particularly due to its proximity to the Dead Sea.
H5044.emploi: Nibschan appears only once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 15:62, in the list of towns attributed to the tribe of Judah during the distribution of the promised lands. The biblical text lists it among six towns in the desert of Judea, indicating that it had some administrative importance, even in an inhospitable region. Its absence from the rest of the Bible suggests that it did not play a major role in the history of Israel, or that its importance was local and limited.

sens: région aride du sud de la Judée
zone semi-désertique
direction du sud
territoire d'Israël
zone de pâturage et de passage
H5045G.detail: 1. The Negev is the mountainous and arid region that extends south of Judea, between Hebron and the Sinai desert. Abraham travels and stays there (Genesis 12:9; 13:1). 2. It is a steppe and semi-desert area, where flocks graze and shepherds find pasture, especially in winter and spring (Psalms 126:4 speaks of streams that flow there). 3. The word literally means "south" or "region of the south": that is why it is also used to designate the southern direction of the territory of Israel. 4. In the conquest narratives, the Negev is an area that the Israelites must dominate, with its fortified cities (Joshua 10:40; 15:21). 5. It is also a crossroads: David and his men operate there, and foreign invasions pass through it (1 Samuel 27:10; 2 Chronicles 28:18).
H5045G.origine: The Hebrew word נֶגֶב (Negev) comes from a root meaning "south" or "to be in the south." It designates both the direction and the region itself — the one that is "to the south" of Jerusalem and Judea. The proper name "Negev" retains this geographical meaning: it is the "land of the south." In Hebrew, negev contrasts with צָפוֹן (tsapon, "north").
H5045G.emploi: The Negev appears 39 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives and conquest texts. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob pass through or reside there (Genesis 12—24). The twelve spies sent for reconnaissance traverse it and report information (Numbers 13). In the conquest of Canaan, the Negev is divided among the tribes, especially Judah and Simeon (Joshua 15; 19). David's narrative mentions it when he operates against the Amalekites (1 Samuel 30). The prophets Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Obadiah cite it in the context of judgment or future restoration. The Negev is both a passageway, a territory to conquer, and a symbol of the south of Israel.
H5045G.portee: The Negev reminds the reader that the Promised Land includes difficult, arid, demanding regions. It symbolizes places of testing and trial where the faith of Abraham and that of the people of Israel were put to the test. It is also a place of concrete inheritance: every topographical detail of the Negev in the Bible affirms that God truly gave land to His people, with its boundaries and resources.

sens: région désertique du sud de la Palestine
direction du sud
côté sud d'un lieu ou d'une construction
H5045H.detail:
1. The Negeb is the desert region that extends south of the Promised Land, between the Dead Sea and the Sinai desert. It is an arid but inhabited territory, with precise geographical limits: in Joshua 15:1-4, the borders of Judah include the Negeb as the southern part of the tribal inheritance.
2. The word also designates the direction of south in general. In Genesis 13:14, God commands Abraham to look to the north, south, east, and west: "Negeb" here simply means south, a cardinal point.
3. In descriptions of the tabernacle and constructions, "negeb" indicates the south side: in Exodus 26:18, the boards of the tabernacle on the side of the negeb (the south) are numbered precisely for construction.
H5045H.origine: The Hebrew word negev likely comes from a root meaning "dry" or "arid," as the Negev is a desert region. Its use has generalized: first the geographical name of the desert in southern Judah, then the word for "south" in general. The same root appears in other Hebrew words related to the dryness and heat of the desert.
H5045H.emploi: The word negeb appears 59 times in the Old Testament, mainly to describe the southern region of Canaan and the territorial delimitations of the tribes. Historical books like Joshua and Samuel use it primarily to geographically situate events and conquests (Joshua 11:2, 15:1-4). Ezekiel uses it intensely to outline the borders of the restored promised land (Ezekiel 48:16-33). Daniel uses it in a geopolitical context, referring to the "king of the Negev" in the wars of the Near East (Daniel 11:5-40). The word is also technical: it precisely indicates the south side of the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 26:18, 1 Kings 7:25).
H5045H.portee: Understanding the Negev helps the reader grasp biblical geography and visualize the narratives of the Old Testament. This arid region also reminds us that God has given a complete land to Israel, even its inhospitable parts, and that He guides His people in all the spaces they occupy.

sens: to make known in words
to report what one has seen or known
to inform someone of news
to declare publicly or solemnly
to confess, to admit
to be made public
H5046.detail:
1. To make known in words: this means to convey information to someone from ear to ear. In Genesis 3:11, God asks Adam, "Who told you that you were naked?" — it is about revealing or telling him something.
2. To report what one has seen or known: a messenger or a witness tells others what has happened. In 1 Samuel 19:19, it is "reported" to Saul that David is in Naioth — it is conveying news that has occurred elsewhere.
3. To inform someone of news: to warn someone of a fact that concerns them. In 2 Samuel 21:11, David is "informed" of what Rizpah has done — important information is communicated to him.
4. To declare publicly or solemnly: to state something in front of witnesses, with the intention of making it an official act. In Joshua 7:19, Joshua asks Achan, "Tell me what you have done" — he orders him to publicly confess his crime.
5. To confess, to admit: to recognize or acknowledge what one has done or what one knows. This is the meaning of the command to Achan to confess his transgression before Israel.
6. To be made public: the passive quality — news becomes known, spreads among the people.
H5046.origine: The Hebrew verb נָגַד comes from a root that evokes the idea of making visible or manifest — "putting before the eyes." It is related to the image of something shining or radiating. In biblical Hebrew, the same family of words includes other verbs of enunciation and publication. This verb is extremely common in Hebrew to express the transmission of words and information between people, and between God and His people.
H5046.emploi: This verb appears more than 300 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis (where it describes conversations and reports among the patriarchs), in historical narratives (Samuel, Kings), and in the Psalms. It covers a wide range: from ordinary conversations (Genesis 24:28, where Rebekah "runs to announce" to her mother) to solemn declarations before God (Joshua 7:19), to religious confessions, and public proclamations. Its meaning varies according to the context: sometimes it is simply "to say" or "to speak," sometimes "to testify" or "to confess," sometimes "to publish" or "to make known to a large number." The verb is at the heart of biblical theology of revelation: God "announces" His acts and His will, and the people must in turn "announce" His wonders.
H5046.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Bible is a book of the transmission of words: what has been heard must be said, what has happened must be reported, what has been hidden must be confessed. It emphasizes the importance of testimony and confession in faith — not only to believe in secret, but to announce, declare, and acknowledge. It is also an invitation to listen: the one who "announces" expects to be heard, and the one who listens has the duty to pass on what they have learned.

sens: To flow continuously, like a liquid that spills
To gush abundantly, to spread
H5047.detail:
1. To flow means to pour out, to spill from one place to another, like water from a river or fountain. In Daniel 7:10, a river of fire "flowed" before the throne of the Most High God: the image evokes a continuous, powerful, and majestic stream emanating from His presence.
2. The word can also express an abundant effusion, an emission that gushes forth without interruption. This is the dynamic of the verb: not a one-time event, but a continuous and irrepressible flow.
H5047.origine: The Hebrew word negad belongs to a family of terms evoking movement and flowing. It describes the physical action of spreading or flowing, which makes its image very concrete and visual. The form used in biblical texts (the Pael or intensive form) reinforces the idea of a vigorous and continuous action.
H5047.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:10, during Daniel's prophetic vision. It describes the river of fire flowing from the divine throne in the heavenly court. It is a term chosen to evoke the power and majesty of God: not only is God seated on His throne, but His presence also emanates a stream of fire that all celestial beings behold in awe-filled worship.
H5047.portee: This image of the flowing river shows that God's glory and justice are not static, immobile: they are alive, dynamic, overflowing. The passage reminds the reader that God reigns with a power that never stops and that His judgment is as irresistible as a stream of fire.

sens: In the position facing something or someone, in front
In the presence of, under the gaze of
In the direction of, towards
In accordance with or parallel to
Contrary to, opposite to
H5048.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to stand or place oneself in front of a person or object, like Hagar who sat "facing" her child at a distance (Genesis 21:16), or Solomon who stood "before" the altar in front of the assembly (2 Chronicles 6:12).
2. To be in the presence of someone, under their gaze or authority: Joshua read the law "in the presence" of the whole assembly (Joshua 8:35), or the burnt offerings are constantly "before" God (Psalms 50:8). It is the idea of being seen, known, judged.
3. To walk in the direction of, to advance towards: the word describes the movement or orientation towards someone.
4. To correspond to or be aligned with: in Nehemiah 12:24, the Levites were "facing" each other, meaning in a parallel or symmetrical position.
5. To face, to oppose: "There is no wisdom or counsel against the Lord" (Proverbs 21:30) means "that can oppose God."
H5048.origine: The Hebrew word négued comes from a root that expresses the idea of "face" or "front." It is a noun that first describes what is visible, in front, and then becomes commonly used as an adverb and preposition. Its use in both the Greek and Hebrew testaments is consistent in expressing position or relationship face to face.
H5048.emploi: The word appears 143 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books and the Psalms. It functions as a noun ("what is before"), adverb ("in front," "before") and preposition ("before," "in the presence of"). Its meaning varies slightly: sometimes purely spatial and concrete (being seated facing someone), sometimes relational and moral (acting "before" the Lord, under His gaze). It frequently appears to express the idea of being in the presence or under the judgment of God, or standing face to face with someone.
H5048.portee: This word invites the believer to remember that they live constantly under the gaze of God. As in the Psalms, where the Lord is always "before" us, the idea is that our life only makes sense when placed in His presence. This calls for sincerity, honesty of heart, and an awareness of the reality of God in our daily lives.

sens: toward, in the direction of
in front of, face to face with
before, in the presence of
H5049.detail:
1. The word indicates the direction toward which one turns or moves: the windows were opened in the direction of Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10), meaning they were turned toward it, as if Daniel wanted to pray by orienting his heart and body toward the holy city.
2. It can mean "in front of" or "face to face with," marking a position or a relationship of facing each other.
3. It expresses the presence before someone or something, the idea of standing forward, visibly, in person.
H5049.origine: This Aramaic word takes the Hebrew form négued (נֶגֶד), which comes from a root meaning "in front of, face to face." The Hebrew family includes notably the verb "to be in front of" and the idea of what stands before oneself. The basic image is that of two things placed in front of each other, facing each other.
H5049.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible in Aramaic, in Daniel 6:10. It designates the precise direction toward which Daniel's windows were opened: Jerusalem. This detail reveals that Daniel's prayer was not secret — his adversaries could see through the open windows that he was praying — and that it was directed toward the holy place, a symbol of God's presence and the heart of Israel's faith, even in exile.
H5049.portee: This word emphasizes the sincerity and clear orientation of prayer: Daniel does not pray in secret or in hiding, but openly, turned toward what represents faithfulness to God. It teaches that praying toward a holy place affirms where our heart is directed and before whom we present ourselves.

sens: To produce or emit light
To illuminate, to light up the darkness
To shine, to radiate brilliance
H5050.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply to produce or emit light: a light source shines when it radiates. This is the image of the stars that "will no longer shine their light" (Isaiah 13:10), or of the fire that will cease to "shine" (Job 18:5).
2. The verb takes on a spiritual dimension when it designates God's action that "illuminates" our darkness (Psalms 18:29, 2 Samuel 22:29): God is not just a source of clarity; He activates light and dispels shadows, illuminating hearts and paths.
3. Thirdly, the word expresses the divine brilliance that "shines" upon the people in darkness (Isaiah 9:1): this is not a passive light, but a glorious and powerful manifestation of divine presence.
H5050.origine: The Hebrew verb נָגַהּ (nagah) belongs to the family of words describing light and brilliance. Its root evokes the fundamental image of emitting light, of radiating. In Hebrew, verbs of this group often express an action that manifests outwardly: to shine means to let the light one carries within show. The word is close to other biblical terms that speak of luminosity and divine clarity.
H5050.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the Old Testament, always in poetry (Psalms and prophecies) or in wisdom sayings (Job). Its use focuses on two axes: first, the natural light that emanates from the stars (Job 18:5, Isaiah 13:10); secondly, and more often, the divine action of spiritual illumination (2 Samuel 22:29, Psalms 18:29, Job 22:28, Isaiah 9:1). In all these contexts, to shine is never neutral: it is a power that acts, that changes, that saves. The verb can designate both the beginning of light and its continuity or intensity.
H5050.portee: This word reveals that divine light is not simply present, but active and communicative. God who "illuminates" our darkness (Psalms 18:29) calls us to recognize His saving action in our lives. For the believer, this means that our paths do not remain dark: God Himself shines upon our steps to guide and transform us. The word invites us to seek less an intellectual clarity than a manifestation of God's presence and power.

sens: Bright and radiant light that shines
Brilliance, shining clarity
Splendor, glorious radiance
Daylight, natural brightness
H5051.detail:
1. The word first designates an intense and radiant light, one that emanates from a bright source. In Ezekiel 1:13, the vision of the heavenly creatures produces a "brilliant light" that bursts forth from the sacred fire circulating among them: it is a visible and striking luminosity.
2. It also describes the resplendence, the clarity that intensifies or grows. Psalm 18:13 shows how divine glory radiates: it is a growing brightness. In Proverbs 4:18, the path of the righteous shines like a light whose "brightness" increases until noon — the image of a clarity that asserts and unfolds.
3. The word carries a strong nuance of splendor, majestic glory. Ezekiel 10:4 speaks of the "splendor" of the glory of the Lord filling the temple courtyard: this is not just a simple light, but a striking manifestation of divine power and holiness.
4. It can also designate the clarity of day, the natural light of the sun. Isaiah 60:3 mentions the "brightness" of the radiant rays toward which the nations walk — a light that illuminates and guides.
H5051.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root expressing the idea of shining, of radiating intensely. It is close to the verb meaning "to be luminous" and belongs to the same family as other biblical terms of splendor and glory. It is a rich word that always paints an active, dynamic light that emanates and spreads — never a simple absence of darkness.
H5051.emploi: The word appears nineteen times in the Old Testament, primarily in the prophetic books (Ezekiel, Isaiah, Amos, Joel, Habakkuk) and the Psalms. It is concentrated in passages where God's glory is visibly manifested: visions of heavenly thrones, theophanies, divine judgments. In 2 Samuel 22:13 and Psalms 18:13, it describes the radiance that precedes God's vengeance. In Proverbs 4:18, it illuminates the moral path of the righteous. In Amos 5:20 and Joel 2:10, the absence of brightness marks the dark judgment of the Lord. The word oscillates between celestial splendor and earthly clarity, but always with a connotation of power and majesty.
H5051.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to perceive divine glory as an active and radiant light, not as a theological abstraction. It emanates, it fills the space, it guides and it judges. Understanding that the brightness of God can both attract the nations (Isaiah 60:3) and be feared (Amos 5:20) reminds us that divine holiness inspires both worship and awe. It is an invitation to walk in this light.

sens: Son of David, king of Israel
One of the thirteen sons born to David in Jerusalem
H5052.detail: 1. Noga is one of the sons of King David, listed among the children that David had during his reign in Jerusalem. His name appears in the genealogical list of royal descendants, indicating his belonging to the established dynastic lineage in Israel.
H5052.origine: The Hebrew name noga literally means "brightness" or "luminosity," evoking the idea of clarity or brilliance. It is a common symbolic name in Israelite royal tradition, which perhaps reflects the hope or favor attached to the birth of a royal child. The genealogical context suggests a prestigious name borne in the house of David.
H5052.emploi: Noga is mentioned twice in the book of Chronicles, always in genealogical lists establishing David's lineage. He appears in 1 Chronicles 3:7, where he is listed among the sons of David born in Jerusalem, and again in 1 Chronicles 14:6, in another similar list of royal children. These two mentions firmly place him in the official genealogy of the royal house of Israel, without any particular account of his life or deeds.

sens: The first light of day, when the sun rises
The moment immediately preceding the sunrise
H5053.detail:
1. Dawn is the brightness that appears in the sky just before the sun rises. It denotes that liminal moment between night and day, when light begins to illuminate the horizon. In Daniel 6:19, the king rises "at the break of day, with the dawn" to rush to the lion's den: he does not wait for the day to be fully risen; he acts at the first light, so great is his anxiety.
2. This word also evokes the general idea of brightness or new light. Dawn symbolizes renewal and the hope that each new day brings with it.
H5053.origine: This Hebrew word (notgah) belongs to the family of words meaning "to shine" or "to radiate." Its Aramaic equivalent nogah is used in Daniel 6:19, attesting that this notion of morning light was well rooted in the thought of the ancient Near East. The basic image is that of brightness emerging from darkness.
H5053.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 6:19. It is a crucial moment in the narrative: King Darius, anxious to know the fate of Daniel thrown into the lion's den the day before, cannot wait for full daylight to go check. At the first light of dawn, he rushes. The context shows that dawn refers to this early moment in the morning when night is barely ending.
H5053.portee: Dawn reminds the reader that each new day brings with it an opportunity for renewal and hope. In the story of Daniel, the king's urgency at dawn shows the strength of human concern and, implicitly, the faithfulness of God who, like a new dawn, brings deliverance after the night of trial.

sens: Bright light, luminous brilliance
Luminosity that allows for clear vision
Figuratively, understanding or truth that dispels ignorance
H5054.detail:
1. The word denotes the brightness or brilliance of light — that which shines and illuminates. In Isaiah 59:9, the people "wait for light" and "brightness," but instead find darkness and gloom: it is indeed the physical light that allows for visibility, used here as an image of deliverance and salvation.
2. Concretely, it is what makes visible, what illuminates a space or landscape. The contrast with darkness shows that it is what shines and lights up.
3. In biblical usage, light and brightness become images of divine deliverance, of God's saving presence. When the people say "we wait for brightness" but walk in darkness, they express their anxious expectation of deliverance and their present disappointment.
H5054.origine: The Hebrew word נְגֹהָה (négohah) comes from a root expressing the idea of shining, radiating. It is a rare word, belonging to poetic and prophetic vocabulary. It is built on roots that express brilliance and luminosity. In the Greek Old Testament, words like λαμπρότης (lamprotès, "splendor") or φῶς (phôs, "light") convey similar ideas.
H5054.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Isaiah 59:9. The context is that of a lamentation of the people — Israel confesses its sins and laments its present state. The prophet enumerates what the people expected (light and brightness, that is, deliverance and blessing) and what they found instead (darkness and gloom, that is, captivity and condemnation). The word thus embodies the messianic hope contrasted by a dark reality.
H5054.portee: This word reminds us that in biblical thought, light and brightness are images of salvation, deliverance, and the blessing presence of God. When Isaiah contrasts it with darkness, he speaks to hearts suffering from the distance of God. For the Christian reader, it also foreshadows how Jesus himself will be called the "Light of the world" — the one who brings true brightness and definitive deliverance.

sens: A blow delivered with horns, generally by an animal
The act of charging and overturning someone with horns
Figuratively: to attack, to defeat, to dominate militarily
H5055.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: an animal (ox, bull, buffalo) gores with its horns. This is what the laws of Deuteronomy describe regarding an ox that gores a man or woman (Exodus 21:28). The animal charges and injures with its horns, which can lead to death.
2. The word also denotes the action of charging with horns to overturn or bring down. Ezekiel 34:21 mentions sheep that gore with their horns to dominate others.
3. Figuratively, "to gore with horns" becomes an image of military power and victory. When Zedekiah makes iron horns and says he will gore the Syrians until they are destroyed (1 Kings 22:11), the horns symbolize the strength that crushes the enemy. Similarly, the horns of Ephraim and Manasseh in Moses' blessing (Deuteronomy 33:17) represent their power to defeat all peoples.
H5055.origine: The Hebrew verb נָגַח comes from a root that evokes the movement of striking with the head or horns. The image is natural: it is the instinctive gesture of an animal using its horns as a weapon. In Hebrew, horns (קֶרֶן, qeren) quickly become a metaphor for strength, power, and dominance, hence the extension of the verb to the military and political domain.
H5055.emploi: The verb appears about 10 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first used literally in the laws of Exodus (21:28, 31, 32): an ox gores with its horns and causes damage. Psalms 44:6 and Ezekiel 34:21 retain a nuance of physical conflict. But from Deuteronomy (33:17) and especially in the prophecies of Daniel and the symbolic acts of the prophets Zedekiah (1 Kings 22:11; 2 Chronicles 18:10), the verb rises to a figurative sense: to gore with horns means to achieve military victory, to crush the enemy. Daniel 8:4 and 11:40 confirm this: the horns of empires represent their military dominance.
H5055.portee: This word reminds us that brute force, even when symbolized by iron horns, is never true power in the eyes of God. The false promises of military victory (that of Zedekiah) contrast with true faith in God's protection. The word also helps to understand the prophetic visions of Daniel regarding empires: their "horns" are merely temporal power, destined to be broken by the eternal God.

H5056.fr: subject to goring (referring to an ox)
sens: Refers to an ox that has a habit of goring
A dangerous animal of which the owner has been warned
A beast known for its harmfulness
H5056.detail:
1. This word describes an ox that has developed the habit of goring with its horns — it is an established character, not an isolated incident. The text in Exodus 21:29 speaks of an ox "that was previously subject to goring": its aggressive behavior has been observed repeatedly; it is its natural tendency.
2. The owner of such an ox is supposed to have been warned — by neighbors, previous victims, or simply by observing the animal's behavior. This knowledge changes all of his legal responsibility.
3. This notion of a beast known for its danger also appears in Exodus 21:36, where "if it is known that the ox was previously subject to goring," the owner who did not supervise the animal must make restitution. The word thus denotes the bad reputation of the animal, its history of violence.
H5056.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the goring action — the characteristic action of the ox that injures. In Hebrew, it is an adjective formed to describe one who has this habit, as one might say "hot-tempered" for someone who has a habit of getting angry. The image is that of the ox lowering its horns and goring, a gesture that has been seen repeated.
H5056.emploi: The word appears only twice, both in the section of Exodus concerning the responsibilities of an owner of an animal that causes damage. In Exodus 21:29, it is the first mention: the ox is "subject to goring" and the owner has been warned. In Exodus 21:36, the same expression "known that the ox was previously subject to goring" establishes the responsibility of the negligent owner. The context is clearly legal: it is the law that governs guilt in cases of death or injury caused by an animal. The key point is that known danger *aggravates* or establishes the owner's guilt.
H5056.portee: This word reminds us that personal responsibility includes monitoring what we own and what can cause harm. The owner who knows that his ox gorges and does not supervise it does not escape justice — knowledge of danger, that is, responsibility. It is a call to caution and honesty: one cannot ignore the risks one creates for others.

sens: One who leads a people or nation as a king or sovereign
One who commands a troop or holds an administrative position
Prince or noble of high rank
That which is remarkable or of great importance
H5057.detail:
1. The leader is primarily one whom God designates to govern His people Israel: David is anointed "leader" of his people (1 Samuel 9:16), just as Solomon is to be "leader" of Israel and Judah (1 Kings 1:35). It is a position of responsibility before God, not merely a political title.
2. The word also designates one who directs the affairs of a city or institution — for example, Conania receives the oversight of the holy offerings (2 Chronicles 31:12), where "leader" means responsible or administrator.
3. It can evoke nobility and power: the "princes" mentioned in the psalm are the mighty of the earth (Psalms 76:13), those who embody political authority.
4. Rarely, it qualifies that which is of great value or major importance, such as remarkable "things" (2 Chronicles 31:12), although this meaning is marginal.
H5057.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to lead" or "to guide." It is related to words that express the idea of guiding or leading a troop. In the Old Testament, the leader is always one whom God establishes or approves — never a mere warrior or band leader: this is why David is called "leader" long before he becomes king, because God chose him.
H5057.emploi: The word appears 44 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Books of Kings and Chronicles, where it designates the kings of Israel and the princes of the house of Judah. It also applies to David and Solomon at their inauguration (1 Samuel 9:16, 1 Kings 1:35), to the officials who manage the temple offerings (2 Chronicles 31:12), and to the nobles who dominate others (Psalms 76:13). The prophet Isaiah applies it to the suffering servant (Isaiah 55:4), presenting him as a leader for the peoples. Daniel uses it for historical powers: the Messiah will be an anointed "leader" (Daniel 9:25), announcing a new kingship.
H5057.portee: The word reminds the believer that the true leader is not one who imposes himself by force, but one whom God establishes and to whom He calls to serve His people. For Israel, recognizing its leader was to recognize the order that God set. For the Christian reading these passages, particularly Daniel's prophecy about the Messiah, the word "leader" evokes legitimate authority — that of Christ — and the call to obey, not out of servile fear, but out of trust in the wisdom of the one whom God has designated.

sens: Stringed musical instruments
Music played on these instruments
Song or chant
Mocking or derisive song
H5058.detail:
1. The word primarily designates musical instruments with strings that are plucked or bowed to produce sounds — such as the harp or lyre. This is the most concrete image: one thinks of the physical object, its vibrating strings. Psalms 6:1 testifies to the "eight-stringed harp."
2. By extension, it designates the music itself produced by these instruments, the sound that emerges from them. Isaiah 38:20 speaks of making "the strings of our instruments resonate" — it is music as it fills the air.
3. The word is also used to refer to a song or chant in general, particularly a song of praise or a psalm. The titles of the Psalms often repeat the expression "stringed instruments," indicating that the psalm should be musically accompanied.
4. Finally, it can evoke a mocking or insulting song. Job 30:9 shows Job as a victim of "songs" of derision — words sung to mock him. It is the same word, but the tone changes: instead of praising God, one mocks.
H5058.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the action of playing a stringed instrument, making the strings vibrate. The family of this word also encompasses the verb "to sing" and "to play music." The basic image is tactile and auditory: fingers that pluck or caress the strings to produce sound. It is a word rooted in the life of the people of Israel, where instrumental music played a central role in worship and celebration.
H5058.emploi: This word appears 14 times in the Old Testament, almost always in the Psalms and in lyrical passages. It is particularly frequent in the titles of the Psalms (Psalms 4, 6, 54, 55, 61, 67, 76) to indicate that they are compositions to be accompanied with stringed instruments. In Lamentations (3:14 and 5:14), the word takes on a darker hue: the songs become songs of mourning or mockery. Isaiah 38:20 uses it in a context of gratitude to God after healing. In any case, the word always evokes the association between music, human emotions (joy, praise, pain, mockery), and the presence of God.
H5058.portee: This word reminds the believer that music and songs are not superfluous ornaments: they are at the heart of the relationship with God. The Psalms were accompanied by instruments, expressing through melody what words alone cannot convey. It is a lesson on the totality of worship: God wants to be worshiped not only by intellect and words, but also by body, by music, by sensory beauty. For the modern reader, this invites a rediscovery of the role of music in faith, far from any empty ceremonialism.

sens: Producing music by striking or plucking the strings of an instrument
Practicing the profession of a musician, playing as a profession
Providing help or relief through music
Accompanying or expressing an emotion through music
H5059.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of making a string instrument sound — harp, lyre, or lute — by striking or plucking it with the hand. David "played with his hand" (1 Samuel 16:23), thus producing the music that soothed Saul.

2. It also refers to one who practices this art: a "harp player" is a professional musician. In 2 Kings 3:15, such a musician is brought in to create the spiritual atmosphere where Elisha can prophesy.

3. Music itself can provide relief: when David played, Saul "breathed easily" and the evil spirit departed from him (1 Samuel 16:23). Music acts here as a force of healing or deliverance.

4. In the Psalms and the prophets, playing an instrument accompanies praise: "Play for him on the harp" (Psalms 33:3) invites expressing joy before God through music.
H5059.origine: The Hebrew root נגן (nagan) comes from a very concrete image: that of striking or plucking strings to produce sound. The word belongs to the family of verbs of precise and ritual movement, such as to vibrate or to pick. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this verb is generally translated by Greek words meaning "to play an instrument" or "to make music." String music was one of the most prestigious forms of musical art in Israel, practiced in temples and royal courts.
H5059.emploi: The verb appears about a dozen times in the Old Testament, mainly concentrated in the story of David at Saul's court (1 Samuel 16-18). It refers to David playing the harp to calm the king's crises. In 2 Kings 3:15, a harp player is brought in before a prophecy, suggesting that music prepares the heart to receive the word of God. The Psalms use it to invite singing and playing in honor of the Lord (Psalms 33:3; 68:26). Isaiah uses it ironically to describe a forgotten woman who "plays pleasantly" (Isaiah 23:16), and to celebrate the praise of the saved (Isaiah 38:20). Ezekiel mentions musicians who "play" before a fascinated audience (Ezekiel 33:32), highlighting the seduction that music can exert.
H5059.portee: This word shows us that music is not merely entertainment in the Bible, but a spiritual force: it can soothe demonic oppression, prepare the heart to hear God, and express praise. David the musician foreshadows the importance of cultivating art and beauty to serve God and others. For today's believer, it is a call to recognize that well-used music is a divine gift that touches the soul and can contribute to healing and sanctification.

sens: To make physical contact with something or someone
To harm someone, to strike or injure
To reach a place, to arrive there or get closer
To occur at a certain moment, to happen
To affect someone with harm or illness
To ritually contaminate by contact
H5060.detail:
1. To touch means to establish direct physical contact with a person or thing: the hand that brushes, grasps, or reaches. This is the simplest action of the word. The angel of the Lord touches Elijah while he is asleep to wake him up (1 Kings 19:7), or Jeremiah feels the hand of God touching his mouth (Jeremiah 1:9) to put the words to say there.
2. To strike or injure: when the word expresses a blow, a violence. The hand of God strikes Job in his trial (Job 19:21), afflicting his body with sores and suffering.
3. To reach a place or get closer: when speaking of distance covered or a limit approached. Jacob's ladder touches heaven in the vision (Genesis 28:12).
4. To occur at a set moment: the word describes what happens, what occurs in the course of time, often destiny or misfortune.
5. To be struck by an illness or plague, to undergo the destructive action of God: Abijah is stricken with an illness that kills him (2 Chronicles 26:20), or Uzziah is struck with leprosy.
6. To contract ritual impurity by simple contact: anyone who touches a corpse becomes unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11), as does anyone who touches certain unclean animals (Leviticus 11:26).
H5060.origine: The Hebrew verb נָגַע (nagaʿ) comes from a root that expresses the idea of making contact, of joining. The primary image is that of the hand reaching out and touching, establishing a physical link with what it encounters. This root has no obvious cognates in other closely related Semitic languages, but it has developed in Hebrew with a rich variety of uses, from simple contact to destructive reaching. The word can also take on the meaning of a calamity that touches you, that is, strikes or affects you with misfortune.
H5060.emploi: This verb appears 142 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Torah (the first five books), the stories of the kings, and the wisdom books. The meaning "to touch" in the physical sense is very common in the purity laws of Leviticus: it refers to touching corpses, unclean animals, and sick persons who render unclean anyone who touches them (Leviticus 11:24-27, Numbers 19:11-13). In history, the word also describes a beneficial contact: the angel touches Elijah to nourish him (1 Kings 19:5-7), God touches Jeremiah's mouth to inspire him (Jeremiah 1:9). The meaning of "to strike" or "to be struck" appears when it involves a divine calamity: an illness strikes, a plague reaches. The word can also mean "to arrive at" or "to reach" in the sense of arriving at a place or accomplishing a distance.
H5060.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that physical contact with God – his touch – can be a source of blessing, comfort, or transformation, as when the angel touches Elijah to strengthen him (1 Kings 19:7). But it also emphasizes that certain things render unclean anyone who approaches them, teaching a reverence for the sacred and a moral awareness of the consequences of our actions. Finally, being "touched" by the hand of God in misfortune is a reality of faith: sometimes the Lord strikes us to correct or test us, and recognizing this hand upon us – whether good or difficult – is the very essence of a life turned toward God.

sens: physical blow, injury or disease that affects the body
visible mark of leprosy or skin infection
disease or plague sent by God as punishment
moral or spiritual suffering
H5061.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a blow or an injury: something that wounds the body and leaves a mark. In Genesis 12:17, the Lord strikes Pharaoh and his house with great plagues — serious diseases that afflict them.
2. In Leviticus, the word specifically applies to the visible mark of leprosy on the skin: in 13:17, the priest examines whether the plague (the leprous spot) has turned white, which signifies healing. It is a mark that can be inspected and diagnosed.
3. In a broader sense, a plague is a scourge — a calamity sent by God as punishment for sin or as judgment. In Deuteronomy 24:8, there is a warning against the plague of leprosy, seen as a divine judgment that the priests must teach to respect.
4. The word can also describe inner suffering or torment of the soul: in Psalms 39:11, the Lord corrects the sinner with plagues (that is, through guilt and remorse) that consume him from within.
H5061.origine: The Hebrew word נֶגַע (nega) comes from a root that means "to touch" or "to strike." It originally describes the blow or physical contact that wounds. The word is closely related to the root נָגַע (naga) (to strike, to reach), which evokes the action of hitting something or someone. This image of violent contact has broadened to include visible marks of disease (especially leprosy) and plagues sent by God.
H5061.emploi: The word appears 62 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in three contexts. First, in the ten plagues of Egypt (Exodus, Genesis 12:17), where it designates the calamities sent by the Lord. Secondly, and by far most frequently, in Leviticus 13-14, where it describes the visible symptoms of leprosy — the spots, tumors, white or reddish areas on the skin — that the priest must examine and diagnose to declare the person clean or unclean. Thirdly, in the Psalms and the prophets, where it represents spiritual suffering or divine punishment: in Psalms 89:33 and 91:10, God threatens to strike the sinner with plagues or promises that the plague will not come near the righteous. In Isaiah 53:8, the man of sorrows is mentioned as bearing our plagues in the sense of our diseases and sufferings.
H5061.portee: This word reminds us that illness and physical suffering are never neutral in the Bible: they reveal something about God, either His judgment on sin or His call to repentance. But it also shows the importance of diagnosis, inspection, and discernment: the priest does not reject the leper without having examined him. For the Christian reader, this word sheds light on the suffering of Jesus in Isaiah 53: He bears our plagues, meaning He takes upon Himself our sickness and our guilt.

sens: To hit someone or something with the hand, a weapon, or an instrument
To inflict a plague, disease, or punishment
To be defeated in battle, to suffer a defeat
To bump into, to collide with an obstacle
To reach, to touch (in the sense of experiencing the effect of)
H5062.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: to deliver a violent blow. Exodus 7:27 speaks of "striking" an entire land with frogs — the image is one of force descending, striking like a blow. It is an act of aggression or punishment.

2. To inflict a plague or disease: "to strike" takes on the meaning of sending a scourge, an epidemic. In 2 Chronicles 21:14, the Lord "will strike" the people with a great plague. The blow becomes invisible but devastating.

3. To be beaten in war, to suffer a military defeat. In 2 Samuel 2:17, the men of Israel "are beaten" by the men of David. Here, "to strike" means to be crushed, to be defeated in battle.

4. To bump into an obstacle, to collide. Proverbs 3:23 says that one will not "strike" their feet — the idea is of a shock against something unexpected.

5. To be affected by something invisible or irreparable. Psalms 91:12 promises that nothing will "strike" you — it is to escape any blow from fate or the enemy.
H5062.origine: The verb נָגַף (nagaf) comes from a Semitic root that evokes the idea of striking, delivering a sudden blow. The basic image is that of a hand coming down, of a force colliding. In the Hebrew Bible, this verb is used for both military blows and plagues sent by God. It is a concrete word at first, which extends metaphorically to anything that "strikes": disease, defeat, misfortune.
H5062.emploi: This verb appears 46 times in the Bible.
